knowledge_statements.title: Unconstrained Smooth Objective Model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional deterministic minimization with globally Lipschitz gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d	o\mathbb{R}\) be continuously differentiable. The unconstrained \(L\)-smooth objective model is
\[\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^d} f(x),\qquad \|
abla f(x)-
abla f(y)\|\le L\|x-y\|\quad	ext{for all }x,y\in\mathbb{R}^d,\]
where \(L>0\). A solution is any \(x^\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb{R}^d}f(x)\), when this set is nonempty. Without convexity, the basic first-order target is instead an \(\varepsilon\)-stationary point satisfying \(\|
abla f(x)\|\le\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize a differentiable function over Euclidean space using a globally Lipschitz gradient; solutions are global minimizers, while nonconvex analysis commonly targets small gradient norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^d}f(x)\) is the unconstrained smooth model, with \(\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|\le L\|x-y\|\).

notation.meaning: global Lipschitz constant of the gradient

children.top_down_role: Objective and gradient information exposed at queried points.

assumptions_latex: Oracle responses are exact and deterministic.

notation.meaning: deterministic update map at iteration k

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact deterministic value-and-gradient oracle for a smooth objective.

source_refs.locator: 1.1 First-order methods in the modern era p. 1
source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(d\in\mathbb{N}\) and a differentiable objective \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\), the exact local first-order oracle is the mapping
\[\mathcal{O}_f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^d,\qquad \mathcal{O}_f(x)=\bigl(f(x),\nabla f(x)\bigr).\]
Given an initial query \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}^d\), a deterministic first-order method may, for each \(k\in\mathbb{N}_0\), generate
\[x_{k+1}=\Phi_k\bigl((x_0,\mathcal{O}_f(x_0)),\ldots,(x_k,\mathcal{O}_f(x_k))\bigr),\]
where \(\Phi_k:(\mathbb{R}^d\times\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^d)^{k+1}\to\mathbb{R}^d\) is a fixed update map. This oracle supplies the objective value and gradient at each queried point, but no Hessian or higher-order derivative information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exact local first-order oracle returns the objective value and gradient at a queried point. A deterministic first-order method chooses each subsequent query through a fixed map of the accumulated query-and-response history.
knowledge_statements.title: Local First-Order Oracle

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Objective Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetric positive-semidefinite quadratics used to expose first-order spectral dynamics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A convex quadratic objective model on \(\mathbb{R}^d\) has the form
\[f(x)=\tfrac12 x^{\mathsf T}Qx-b^{\mathsf T}x+c,\qquad Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\succeq0,\]
with gradient \(\nabla f(x)=Qx-b\). It is \(L\)-smooth when \(\lambda_{\max}(Q)\le L\), and it is \(\mu\)-strongly convex when \(Q\succeq\mu I\) for some \(\mu>0\). A minimizer exists exactly when \(b\in\operatorname{range}(Q)\), in which case every minimizer solves \(Qx^\star=b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex quadratic is determined by a symmetric positive-semidefinite Hessian. Its extreme eigenvalues control smoothness and strong convexity, and minimizers solve the associated linear system.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\) is symmetric and positive semidefinite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla f(x)=Qx-b\), with smoothness and curvature determined by the spectrum of \(Q\).

children.title: Quadratic Momentum Stability
children.top_down_role: Stable, oscillatory, and divergent momentum regimes on quadratic objectives.

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Momentum Stability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Schur-stability condition for constant-parameter heavy-ball dynamics on positive-definite quadratics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the heavy-ball iteration
\[x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha(Qx_k-b)+\beta(x_k-x_{k-1})\]
on a quadratic with \(Q\succ0\), the error in an eigendirection of eigenvalue \(\lambda\) obeys
\[z_{k+1}=(1+\beta-\alpha\lambda)z_k-\beta z_{k-1}.\]
This mode is asymptotically stable exactly when both roots of
\[r^2-(1+\beta-\alpha\lambda)r+\beta=0\]
lie in the open unit disk. For real parameters, the equivalent inequalities are \(|\beta|<1\), \(\alpha\lambda>0\), and \(\alpha\lambda<2(1+\beta)\). Stability on the entire spectrum requires these inequalities for every \(\lambda\in\operatorname{spec}(Q)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Heavy-ball stability reduces to a second-order scalar recurrence in each eigendirection. All characteristic roots must lie strictly inside the unit disk for every eigenvalue.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Quadratic momentum is stable exactly when \(|\beta|<1\), \(0<\alpha\lambda<2(1+\beta)\) for every \(\lambda\in\operatorname{spec}(Q)\).

notation.meaning: characteristic root of an eigenmode recurrence

children.title: Local Quadratic Upper Models
children.top_down_role: Local models supporting backtracking and local smoothness adaptation.

assumptions_latex: For the sufficient-condition statement, \(\nabla f\) is \(L_{x,y}\)-Lipschitz on a neighborhood of the segment joining \(x\) and \(y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The trial point \(y\) satisfies the local upper-model test when \(f(y)\le Q_M(y;x)\); this test is guaranteed when \(M\ge L_{x,y}\).

notation.meaning: quadratic model of f at x with trial curvature M

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Trial-point majorization condition used by backtracking line search.

source_refs.locator: 10.3 Analysis of the Proximal Gradient Method-The Nonconvex Case p. 272
source_refs.source_title: First-Order Methods in Optimization

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(d\in\mathbb{N}\), a differentiable function \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\), a base point \(x\in\mathbb{R}^d\), and a trial curvature \(M>0\), define
\[Q_M(y;x)=f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle+\frac{M}{2}\|y-x\|^2.\]
A trial point \(y\in\mathbb{R}^d\) satisfies the local quadratic upper-model condition when
\[f(y)\le Q_M(y;x).\]
If \(\nabla f\) is \(L_{x,y}\)-Lipschitz on a neighborhood of the segment joining \(x\) and \(y\), then the condition holds whenever \(M\ge L_{x,y}\). In gradient backtracking, one may test \(y_M=x-M^{-1}\nabla f(x)\) and increase \(M\) until the displayed condition holds. If \(\nabla f\) is Lipschitz on a fixed neighborhood of \(x\), then this procedure accepts for all sufficiently large \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local quadratic upper-model test compares the objective at a proposed point with a quadratic model based at the current point. A Lipschitz constant valid near the tested segment guarantees the test when the trial curvature is at least that constant; local Lipschitz continuity near the base point therefore ensures eventual acceptance by gradient backtracking.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Quadratic Upper Models

knowledge_statements.title: Cocoercive Gradient View
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Baillon–Haddad inequality in finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d	o\mathbb{R}\) be convex and differentiable with an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient. Then its gradient is \(1/L\)-cocoercive:
\[\langle
abla f(x)-
abla f(y),x-yangle\ge rac{1}{L}\|
abla f(x)-
abla f(y)\|^2\qquad	ext{for all }x,y\in\mathbb{R}^d.\]
Equivalently, the scaled gradient mapping \(L^{-1}
abla f\) is firmly nonexpansive. In particular, \(
abla f\) is monotone and \(L\)-Lipschitz, with the displayed inequality coupling these two properties more strongly than either alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The gradient of a convex smooth function is cocoercive: its directional monotonicity dominates the squared difference of gradients scaled by the reciprocal smoothness constant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\(\langle
abla f(x)-
abla f(y),x-yangle\ge L^{-1}\|
abla f(x)-

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(d\in\mathbb{N}\). If \(f:\mathbb{R}^d	o\mathbb{R}\) is convex and differentiable with an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, where \(L>0\), then for all \(x,y\in\mathbb{R}^d\),
\[f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle
abla f(x),y-xangle+ rac{1}{2L}\|
abla f(y)-
abla f(x)\|^2.\]
Thus the affine lower bound from convexity admits a nonnegative gradient-difference correction. If a minimizer \(x^\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{u\in\mathbb{R}^d}f(u)\) exists, taking \(x=x^\star\) and \(y=u\), and using \(
abla f(x^\star)=0\), gives
\[f(u)-f(x^\star)\ge rac{1}{2L}\|
abla f(u)\|^2\qquad	ext{for all }u\in\mathbb{R}^d.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Smooth convexity strengthens the affine support inequality by a squared gradient-difference term. Applying this inequality with the minimizer as the base point shows that objective suboptimality controls the squared gradient norm.

children.title: Smooth Nonconvex Regime

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Nonconvex Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth minimization without convexity, measured by first-order stationarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The smooth nonconvex regime consists of objectives \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) that are differentiable, bounded below, and have an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, without requiring convexity. A point \(x\) is first-order stationary when
\[\nabla f(x)=0,\]
and is \(\varepsilon\)-stationary when
\[\|\nabla f(x)\|\le\varepsilon.\]
Because stationarity need not imply global or local optimality, the canonical global performance criterion for a first-order algorithm is reduction of \(\min_{0\le k<K}\|\nabla f(x_k)\|\), rather than a guaranteed global objective gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without convexity, smooth first-order analysis targets points with small gradient. Such stationarity does not by itself certify local or global optimality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The regime uses \(\|\nabla f(x)\|\le\varepsilon\) as its standard approximate-solution criterion.

children.title: Smooth Convex Regime
children.top_down_role: Global objective-gap analysis under convexity.

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Convex Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex smooth minimization measured by global objective suboptimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The smooth convex regime consists of differentiable functions \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) satisfying
\[f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in\mathbb{R}^d\]
and
\[\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|\le L\|x-y\|\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in\mathbb{R}^d.\]
When \(X^\star=\operatorname*{argmin}f\) is nonempty, the canonical accuracy criterion is the global gap \(f(x)-f^\star\le\varepsilon\), where \(f^\star=\min f\). Every stationary point is then a global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convexity turns first-order stationarity into global optimality. Algorithmic accuracy is naturally measured by objective value above the global minimum.
assumptions_latex: \(X^\star\ne\varnothing\) when an objective-gap criterion is invoked.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla f(x)=0\) implies \(x\in X^\star\), and accuracy may be measured by \(f(x)-f^\star\le\varepsilon\).

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Strongly Convex Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth strongly convex minimization with finite condition number and unique minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The \((\mu,L)\)-smooth strongly convex regime consists of differentiable functions \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) such that, for all \(x,y\in\mathbb{R}^d\),
\[f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle+\frac{\mu}{2}\|y-x\|^2\]
and
\[\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|\le L\|x-y\|,\]
where \(0<\mu\le L\). Such an objective has at most one minimizer; when a minimizer \(x^\star\) exists, it is unique. The ratio \(\kappa=L/\mu\) is the condition number governing standard first-order contraction factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong convexity adds uniform positive curvature to smooth convexity, yielding a unique minimizer when attained and a finite condition number controlling first-order convergence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The model is simultaneously \(\mu\)-strongly convex and \(L\)-smooth, with condition number \(\kappa=L/\mu\).

knowledge_statements.title: Polyak-Lojasiewicz Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global Polyak–Łojasiewicz gradient dominance for a differentiable objective with an attained minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable, let \(f^*=\min_x f(x)\), and assume the minimum is attained. The function satisfies the Polyak–Łojasiewicz condition with constant \(\mu>0\) when
\[
\frac{1}{2}\lVert\nabla f(x)\rVert_2^2\geq \mu\bigl(f(x)-f^*\bigr)\qquad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb{R}^n.
\]
Consequently, every stationary point is globally minimizing, although the condition alone does not require \(f\) to be convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: PL geometry bounds objective suboptimality by the squared gradient norm, so every stationary point is a global minimizer without requiring convexity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\frac12\lVert\nabla f(x)\rVert_2^2\geq\mu(f(x)-f^*)\) for all \(x\), hence \(\nabla f(x)=0\Rightarrow f(x)=f^*\).

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic-Growth Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global quadratic growth measured by Euclidean distance to the minimizer set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) have finite attained minimum \(f^*\), and write \(X^*=\operatorname*{argmin} f\neq\varnothing\). The function has quadratic growth with modulus \(\mu>0\) on a set \(D\subseteq\operatorname{dom}f\) when
\[
f(x)-f^*\geq \frac{\mu}{2}\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)^2\qquad\text{for every }x\in D.
\]
Taking \(D=\operatorname{dom}f\) gives global quadratic growth; choosing a neighborhood of \(X^*\) gives the local form.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic growth lower-bounds objective error by a positive multiple of squared distance to the solution set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)-f^*\geq(\mu/2)\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)^2\) for every \(x\in D\).

knowledge_statements.title: Residual Error-Bound Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gradient-residual error bound for unconstrained differentiable minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable with nonempty minimizer set \(X^*=\operatorname*{argmin}f\). A gradient-residual error bound holds on \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) with constant \(\kappa>0\) when
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\leq \kappa\lVert\nabla f(x)\rVert_2\qquad\text{for every }x\in D.
\]
The condition is global when \(D=\mathbb{R}^n\), and local when \(D\) is a specified neighborhood or objective sublevel set containing \(X^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The gradient-residual error bound controls distance to the minimizer set by the gradient norm on a specified region.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\leq\kappa\lVert\nabla f(x)\rVert_2\) for every \(x\in D\).

notation.meaning: Region on which the error bound holds.

children.title: Growth–Error-Bound Equivalence Regimes
children.top_down_role: Settings where growth properties support comparable residual-based control.

knowledge_statements.title: Growth–Error-Bound Equivalence Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existential equivalence for convex differentiable objectives; constants need not be sharp.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex and continuously differentiable, with nonempty closed minimizer set \(X^*\) and finite value \(f^*\). Suppose \(\nabla f\) is globally Lipschitz. Then the following global properties are equivalent: there exists \(\mu>0\) such that
\[
f(x)-f^*\geq\frac{\mu}{2}\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)^2,
\]
and there exists \(\kappa>0\) such that
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\leq\kappa\lVert\nabla f(x)\rVert_2.
\]
Both inequalities are required for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\); the analogous equivalence holds on compatible invariant sublevel regions under corresponding local hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For convex smooth objectives, global quadratic growth is equivalent to a global gradient-residual error bound, up to changes in constants.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex and continuously differentiable on \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists\mu>0\) satisfying quadratic growth if and only if \(\exists\kappa>0\) satisfying the gradient-residual error bound.
review_flags: exact equivalence hypotheses and localization regime require authoritative source confirmation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The global equivalence is plausible under the stated convex smooth hypotheses, but its exact assumptions and constants require authoritative confirmation. knowledge_statements.title: Euclidean Gradient Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Riesz-gradient and steepest quadratic-model representation in finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For differentiable \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), the Euclidean gradient \(g=\nabla f(x)\) is the unique vector satisfying \(Df(x)[d]=\langle g,d\rangle_2\) for every direction \(d\). For any \(\alpha>0\), the Euclidean gradient step is equivalently characterized by
\[
d_x=\operatorname*{argmin}_{d\in\mathbb{R}^n}\left\{\langle g,d\rangle_2+\frac{1}{2\alpha}\lVert d\rVert_2^2\right\}=-\alpha g.
\]
Thus the gradient identifies the locally steepest direction under the Euclidean quadratic penalty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Euclidean gradient represents the derivative, and its negative scaled value uniquely minimizes the regularized local linear model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Df(x)[d]=\langle\nabla f(x),d\rangle_2\) and \(d_x=-\alpha\nabla f(x)\).

notation.meaning: Directional action of the derivative at x on d.

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Euclidean Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed symmetric positive-definite metric and its preconditioned gradient representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) be symmetric positive definite. Define \(\langle u,v\rangle_M=u^{\mathsf T}Mv\), \(\lVert u\rVert_M=(u^{\mathsf T}Mu)^{1/2}\), and the dual norm \(\lVert g\rVert_{M^{-1}}=(g^{\mathsf T}M^{-1}g)^{1/2}\). For differentiable \(f\), its metric gradient is \(\operatorname{grad}_M f(x)=M^{-1}\nabla f(x)\), and
\[
\operatorname*{argmin}_{d}\left\{\langle\nabla f(x),d\rangle_2+\frac{1}{2\alpha}\lVert d\rVert_M^2\right\}=-\alpha M^{-1}\nabla f(x).
\]
Hence a fixed metric acts as a fixed preconditioner.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-definite metric replaces the Euclidean gradient by the preconditioned vector obtained by applying the inverse metric matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{grad}_M f(x)=M^{-1}\nabla f(x)\) and the metric step equals \(-\alpha M^{-1}\nabla f(x)\).

notation.meaning: Gradient relative to the M-inner product.

knowledge_statements.title: General-Norm Steepest Descent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Steepest regularized direction under an arbitrary finite-dimensional norm and its dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\lVert\cdot\rVert\) be a norm on \(\mathbb{R}^n\), with dual norm \(\lVert g\rVert_*\). Given \(g=\nabla f(x)\) and \(\alpha>0\), choose
\[
d_x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{d\in\mathbb{R}^n}\left\{\langle g,d\rangle+\frac{1}{2\alpha}\lVert d\rVert^2\right\}.
\]
Every such direction satisfies \(\lVert d_x\rVert=\alpha\lVert g\rVert_*\), \(\langle g,d_x\rangle=-\alpha\lVert g\rVert_*^2\), and the minimum model value is \(-\alpha\lVert g\rVert_*^2/2\). The direction may be nonunique when the squared norm is not strictly convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: General-norm steepest descent minimizes a linearized objective plus squared norm penalty, with direction magnitude governed by the dual gradient norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_x\) minimizes the regularized linear model and satisfies \(\lVert d_x\rVert=\alpha\lVert\nabla f(x)\rVert_*\).

notation.meaning: Dual norm of the chosen primal norm.
Derivative represented in the standard dual pairing.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input a differentiable objective \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), an initial point \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}^n\), positive stepsizes \((\alpha_k)_{k\geq0}\), and a stopping tolerance \(\varepsilon\geq0\). At iteration \(k\), evaluate \(g_k=\nabla f(x_k)\). If \(\lVert g_k\rVert_2\leq\varepsilon\), output \(x_k\); otherwise set
\[
x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_k g_k
\]
and continue. If no finite stopping time occurs, the output is the generated sequence \((x_k)_{k\geq0}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gradient descent repeatedly subtracts a positive stepsize times the exact Euclidean gradient and stops when the gradient norm meets tolerance.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input differentiable \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}^n\), a fixed matrix \(M=M^{\mathsf T}\succ0\), positive stepsizes \((\alpha_k)\), and tolerance \(\varepsilon\geq0\). At iteration \(k\), compute \(g_k=\nabla f(x_k)\). If \(\lVert g_k\rVert_{M^{-1}}\leq\varepsilon\), output \(x_k\); otherwise compute the unique metric direction
\[
d_k=\operatorname*{argmin}_d\left\{\langle g_k,d\rangle_2+\frac12\lVert d\rVert_M^2\right\}=-M^{-1}g_k
\]
and update \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_k d_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric steepest descent applies the inverse fixed metric to the exact gradient before taking each prescribed step.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) have an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, and apply \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha\nabla f(x_k)\) with a constant \(\alpha\in(0,2/L)\). Then the smoothness inequality gives
\[
f(x_{k+1})\leq f(x_k)-\alpha\left(1-\frac{L\alpha}{2}\right)\lVert\nabla f(x_k)\rVert_2^2.
\]
In particular, \(\alpha=1/L\) yields \(f(x_{k+1})\leq f(x_k)-\lVert\nabla f(x_k)\rVert_2^2/(2L)\). No convexity is required for this one-step descent guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any constant step below twice the reciprocal smoothness yields objective descent; the standard reciprocal-smoothness step gives a simple gradient-square decrease.

children.title: Diminishing Stepsize Schedules

knowledge_statements.title: Diminishing Stepsize Schedules
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonsummable diminishing schedules for smooth convex deterministic gradient descent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A positive stepsize sequence \((\alpha_k)_{k\geq0}\) is a diminishing nonsummable schedule when
\[
\alpha_k>0,\qquad \alpha_k\to0,\qquad \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\alpha_k=+\infty.
\]
For an \(L\)-smooth convex objective, a smooth deterministic specialization additionally imposes \(\alpha_k\leq1/L\). A standard polynomial family is \(\alpha_k=a/(k+b)^p\), where \(a>0\), \(b>0\), and \(0<p\leq1\), with \(a/b^p\leq1/L\). If square summability is also required, then \(p>1/2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Diminishing schedules stay positive, converge to zero, and have divergent total length; polynomial schedules characterize when square summability also holds.
assumptions_latex: \(L>0\) when the smooth deterministic cap is imposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha_k\to0\) while \(\sum_k\alpha_k=+\infty\); for \(p>1/2\), also \(\sum_k\alpha_k^2<+\infty\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact-target Polyak steps for differentiable convex minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input a differentiable convex objective \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), an initial point \(x_0\), and the known optimal value \(f^*=\min_x f(x)\). At iteration \(k\), compute \(g_k=\nabla f(x_k)\). If \(g_k=0\), output \(x_k\); otherwise set
\[
\alpha_k=\frac{f(x_k)-f^*}{\lVert g_k\rVert_2^2},
\qquad
x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_k g_k.
\]
The rule therefore requires an exact objective value and the target \(f^*\); replacing \(f^*\) by an estimate defines a different target-value policy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Polyak rule divides current objective error by squared gradient norm and therefore requires knowledge of the optimal target value.

children.title: Exact Line Search

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Line Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unconstrained exact minimization along a fixed descent ray.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), let \(x_k\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and choose \(p_k\in\mathbb{R}^n\) with \(\nabla f(x_k)^\top p_k<0\). Define \(\phi_k(\alpha)=f(x_k+\alpha p_k)\) for \(\alpha\ge 0\). Exact line search selects any
\[
\alpha_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\alpha\ge 0}\phi_k(\alpha)
\]
and outputs \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kp_k\). The update is defined only when this argmin is nonempty. If \(\alpha_k>0\), \(f\) is differentiable, and \(\alpha_k\) is an interior minimizer, then \(\phi_k'(\alpha_k)=\nabla f(x_k+\alpha_kp_k)^\top p_k=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize the objective exactly along the chosen descent ray, then update by the minimizing step. Any interior minimizer makes the new gradient orthogonal to the search direction.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable on an open set containing \(\{x_k+\alpha p_k:\alpha\ge0\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kp_k\), where \(\alpha_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\alpha\ge0}f(x_k+\alpha p_k)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Interpolation Line Search

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\phi(\alpha)=f(x+\alpha p)\), and suppose values \(\phi(\alpha_i)\) and, when available, derivatives \(\phi'(\alpha_i)\) have been sampled. At each iteration construct a quadratic or cubic polynomial \(q\) interpolating the selected data. Compute a model minimizer \(\widehat\alpha\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\alpha\in I}q(\alpha)\), then safeguard it by choosing \(\alpha^+\in I_{\mathrm{safe}}\subseteq I\), using \(\widehat\alpha\) when it lies in \(I_{\mathrm{safe}}\) and a prescribed fallback otherwise. Evaluate \(\phi(\alpha^+)\), update the sampled data and interval, and stop when the governing line-search acceptance condition holds; output \(\alpha^+\).

children.title: Armijo Backtracking
children.top_down_role: Backtracking globalization based on sufficient decrease.

knowledge_statements.title: Armijo Backtracking
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric backtracking until Armijo sufficient decrease holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x_k\in\mathbb{R}^n\), a direction \(p_k\) satisfying \(g_k^\top p_k<0\), parameters \(c\in(0,1)\), \(\rho\in(0,1)\), and an initial trial \(\bar\alpha>0\), initialize \(\alpha\leftarrow\bar\alpha\). While
\[
f(x_k+\alpha p_k)>f(x_k)+c\alpha g_k^\top p_k,
\]
replace \(\alpha\leftarrow\rho\alpha\). On termination set \(\alpha_k=\alpha\) and output \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kp_k\). If \(f\) is continuously differentiable near \(x_k\), the loop terminates after finitely many reductions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly shrink an initial positive step by a fixed factor until the objective achieves Armijo sufficient decrease, then accept the resulting iterate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A finite backtracking index \(j\ge0\) exists with \(\alpha_k=\bar\alpha\rho^j\) satisfying \(f(x_k+\alpha_kp_k)\le f(x_k)+c\alpha_kg_k^\top p_k\).

children.title: Goldstein Search

knowledge_statements.title: Goldstein Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical two-sided sufficient-decrease condition for a descent direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable, let \(x_k,p_k\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and suppose \(g_k^\top p_k<0\), where \(g_k=\nabla f(x_k)\). For a parameter \(c\in(0,\tfrac12)\), a step \(\alpha_k>0\) satisfies the Goldstein conditions when
\[
f(x_k)+(1-c)\alpha_k g_k^\top p_k
\le f(x_k+\alpha_kp_k)
\le f(x_k)+c\alpha_k g_k^\top p_k.
\]
The right inequality requires sufficient decrease, while the left inequality excludes steps whose decrease is excessively large relative to the first-order model, thereby preventing an unnecessarily short accepted step.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Accept a positive step only when its objective value lies between two affine bounds based on the initial directional derivative.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable along \(x_k+\alpha p_k\) for relevant \(\alpha\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha_k\) is Goldstein-acceptable exactly when the displayed two-sided inequalities hold.

children.title: Nonmonotone Line Search

knowledge_statements.title: Nonmonotone Line Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Windowed Armijo acceptance using recent objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix an integer memory length \(M\ge1\). At iteration \(k\), define \(m_k=\min\{M-1,k\}\) and the reference value
\[
F_k=\max_{0\le j\le m_k}f(x_{k-j}).
\]
For a descent direction \(p_k\), with \(g_k=\nabla f(x_k)\) and \(g_k^\top p_k<0\), a trial step \(\alpha_k>0\) is accepted when
\[
f(x_k+\alpha_kp_k)\le F_k+c\alpha_k g_k^\top p_k,
\]
where \(c\in(0,1)\). Because \(F_k\ge f(x_k)\), an accepted step may increase the objective relative to \(f(x_k)\), but only relative to the controlled window reference.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use the largest objective among recent iterates as the Armijo reference, allowing controlled one-step increases while enforcing decrease relative to that window.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The step is accepted if \(f(x_k+\alpha_kp_k)\le F_k+c\alpha_k g_k^\top p_k\).

notation.meaning: maximum number of recent objective values in the window
available memory length at iteration k

knowledge_statements.title: Wolfe Line Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak Wolfe sufficient-decrease and curvature conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuously differentiable, let \(x_k,p_k\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and suppose \(g_k^\top p_k<0\), where \(g_k=\nabla f(x_k)\). Given \(0<c_1<c_2<1\), a step \(\alpha_k>0\) satisfies the Wolfe conditions if
\[
f(x_k+\alpha_kp_k)\le f(x_k)+c_1\alpha_k g_k^\top p_k
\]
and
\[
\nabla f(x_k+\alpha_kp_k)^\top p_k\ge c_2 g_k^\top p_k.
\]
The first inequality imposes sufficient decrease; the second requires the directional derivative to have increased sufficiently from its negative initial value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Wolfe step provides Armijo decrease and makes the new directional derivative sufficiently less negative than its initial value.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is continuously differentiable along the relevant search ray.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha_k\) is Wolfe-acceptable exactly when both displayed inequalities hold.

children.title: Strong Wolfe Line Search

knowledge_statements.title: Strong Wolfe Line Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong Wolfe acceptance with absolute directional-curvature control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuously differentiable, let \(x_k,p_k\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and suppose \(g_k^\top p_k<0\), where \(g_k=\nabla f(x_k)\). Given \(0<c_1<c_2<1\), a step \(\alpha_k>0\) satisfies the strong Wolfe conditions if
\[
f(x_k+\alpha_kp_k)\le f(x_k)+c_1\alpha_k g_k^\top p_k
\]
and
\[
\left|\nabla f(x_k+\alpha_kp_k)^\top p_k\right|\le c_2\left|g_k^\top p_k\right|.
\]
Thus the accepted point has sufficient decrease and a directional derivative whose magnitude is reduced by at least the prescribed factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strong Wolfe step gives Armijo decrease and bounds the magnitude of the new directional derivative by a fraction of its initial magnitude.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is continuously differentiable along the relevant search ray.

children.title: Bracket-Refinement Calculus

children.title: Trial-Step Bracketing

knowledge_statements.title: Trial-Step Bracketing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bracketing phase for a strong-Wolfe line search, including the finite step-limit outcome.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\phi(\alpha)=f(x+\alpha p)\), where \(\phi'(0)<0\), and choose \(0<c_1<c_2<1\). Starting with \(\alpha_0=0\), evaluate an increasing sequence of positive trials \(\alpha_i\). Invoke interval refinement on \([\alpha_{i-1},\alpha_i]\) if \(\phi(\alpha_i)>\phi(0)+c_1\alpha_i\phi'(0)\), or if \(i>1\) and \(\phi(\alpha_i)\ge\phi(\alpha_{i-1})\). Accept \(\alpha_i\) if \(|\phi'(\alpha_i)|\le -c_2\phi'(0)\). If \(\phi'(\alpha_i)\ge0\), invoke interval refinement on \([\alpha_i,\alpha_{i-1}]\). Otherwise choose a larger safeguarded trial and continue. If no larger admissible trial exists because the prescribed maximum step or evaluation limit has been reached, terminate with an unsuccessful bracketing status rather than certify the strong Wolfe conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Increase trial steps until one satisfies the strong Wolfe conditions, two sampled steps form an interval for refinement, or a prescribed step or evaluation limit forces an explicit unsuccessful exit.
assumptions_latex: \(\phi\) is continuously differentiable on every interval evaluated by the procedure and \(\phi'(0)<0\).
Positive trials increase according to a prescribed safeguard and are subject to declared step and evaluation limits.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The phase returns either a strong-Wolfe step, two endpoints for interval refinement, or an explicit unsuccessful status caused by a declared implementation limit.

children.title: Zoom Interval Refinement
children.top_down_role: Progressive restriction of a valid search interval.

knowledge_statements.title: Zoom Interval Refinement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Safeguarded interval refinement for strong-Wolfe acceptance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given endpoints \(\alpha_{\mathrm{lo}}\) and \(\alpha_{\mathrm{hi}}\) that bracket a strong-Wolfe search, repeatedly choose a safeguarded trial \(\alpha_j\) strictly between them. If \(\phi(\alpha_j)>\phi(0)+c_1\alpha_j\phi'(0)\) or \(\phi(\alpha_j)\ge\phi(\alpha_{\mathrm{lo}})\), set \(\alpha_{\mathrm{hi}}\leftarrow\alpha_j\). Otherwise, accept \(\alpha_j\) when \(|\phi'(\alpha_j)|\le-c_2\phi'(0)\). If it is not accepted and \(\phi'(\alpha_j)(\alpha_{\mathrm{hi}}-\alpha_{\mathrm{lo}})\ge0\), first set \(\alpha_{\mathrm{hi}}\leftarrow\alpha_{\mathrm{lo}}\); then set \(\alpha_{\mathrm{lo}}\leftarrow\alpha_j\). Stop upon acceptance or a declared interval or evaluation tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Refine a bracket with safeguarded interior trials, preserving the strong-Wolfe bracketing logic until acceptance or a declared numerical tolerance.
assumptions_latex: The supplied endpoints satisfy the bracketing invariants of the strong-Wolfe search.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure returns a strong-Wolfe step when its acceptance test succeeds; otherwise it reports termination at the prescribed tolerance.

children.title: Bracket Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Degenerate intervals, unsuccessful expansion, and unreliable evaluations during interval management.

knowledge_statements.title: Bracket Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions under which finite bracketing or reliable refinement is not guaranteed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A bracketing line search cannot guarantee a finite accepted step from its usual continuity argument if the initial direction is not descent, namely \(\phi'(0)\ge0\), or if \(\phi\) or \(\phi'\) is unavailable or discontinuous on the searched interval. Even with smooth \(\phi\) and \(\phi'(0)<0\), an implementation may fail operationally when a finite maximum step prevents reaching a valid bracket, evaluation limits are exhausted, nonfinite function values occur, or floating-point trials cease to be distinct. In these cases it must report failure or invoke a documented fallback; it must not claim that the requested Wolfe conditions were certified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bracketing guarantees break without a descent derivative or adequate regularity; finite bounds, evaluation limits, nonfinite values, and floating-point collapse also require explicit failure handling.
assumptions_latex: The target acceptance rule is a Wolfe-type line-search condition.
The implementation uses finitely representable trial steps and finite evaluation budgets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If any stated failure mechanism occurs before acceptance, Wolfe acceptance is uncertified and the routine must return failure or a documented fallback result.

children.title: Trial-Step Safeguard Calculus
children.top_down_role: Bounds and fallback mechanisms for trial-step generation.

children.title: Interpolation Trial Safeguards
children.top_down_role: Bounds controlling model-based trial points inside a search interval.

knowledge_statements.title: Interpolation Trial Safeguards
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interior-margin safeguard for interpolation-generated trial steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let the current bracket be \([a,b]\) with \(a<b\), and fix a margin parameter \(\delta\in(0,\tfrac12)\). If polynomial interpolation proposes \(\widehat\alpha\), the proposal is admissible only when
\[
a+\delta(b-a)\le\widehat\alpha\le b-\delta(b-a).
\]
Otherwise replace it by a fallback \(\alpha_{\mathrm{fb}}\) in the same safeguarded interval, for example its midpoint. Consequently every accepted trial \(\alpha^+\) satisfies
\[
\min\{\alpha^+-a,b-\alpha^+\}\ge\delta(b-a),
\]
so refinement cannot repeatedly select a trial arbitrarily close to an endpoint solely because an interpolating polynomial is ill-conditioned or has an unsuitable minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Accept an interpolated trial only inside a fixed interior portion of the bracket; otherwise use an interior fallback such as bisection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every selected trial \(\alpha^+\) remains at least \(\delta(b-a)\) from either bracket endpoint.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The interior-margin condition is internally correct, but the fixed relative margin and fallback policy define a particular implementation-dependent safeguard. No authoritative source or locator is supplied for that parameterization.

children.title: Extrapolation Trial Safeguards
children.top_down_role: Limits controlling trial points beyond previously evaluated steps.

knowledge_statements.title: Extrapolation Trial Safeguards
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded-expansion safeguard for trials outside the sampled range.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose the largest sampled step is \(b>0\), the preceding sampled step is \(a\in[0,b)\), and extrapolation proposes \(\widehat\alpha>b\). Fix expansion factors \(1<\gamma_{\min}\le\gamma_{\max}<\infty\) and an optional maximum step \(\alpha_{\max}>b\). Select
\[
\alpha^+\in[\,b+\gamma_{\min}(b-a),\ b+\gamma_{\max}(b-a)\,]\cap( b,\alpha_{\max}].
\]
If this set is empty, report the step-limit boundary instead of extrapolating. Thus each successful extrapolation makes positive progress beyond \(b\) while preventing an unbounded jump caused by an unreliable model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Force extrapolated trials to expand beyond the current sample by controlled minimum and maximum factors, while respecting a prescribed maximum step.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A successful trial \(\alpha^+\) lies beyond \(b\), within the bounded expansion interval, and no greater than \(\alpha_{\max}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bounded-expansion rule is mathematically coherent, including its empty-intersection boundary, but its expansion-factor parameterization is implementation dependent and has no cited authoritative source or locator.

children.title: Fallback Trial Selection
children.top_down_role: Conservative trial choices used when model-based proposals are unreliable.

knowledge_statements.title: Fallback Trial Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Safeguarded bisection fallback when an interpolation or extrapolation trial is invalid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a valid bracket with endpoints \(0\leq a<b\), safeguard parameter \(\delta\in(0,1/2)\), and proposed trial \(\widehat\alpha\), define \(I_\delta=[a+\delta(b-a),\,b-\delta(b-a)]\). If \(\widehat\alpha\) is finite and belongs to \(I_\delta\), select \(\alpha=\widehat\alpha\); otherwise select the fallback \(\alpha=(a+b)/2\). Evaluate the line-search function and any required directional derivative at \(\alpha\), then update the bracket according to the chosen acceptance conditions. The fallback lies strictly inside the bracket and reduces its length by one half when it becomes the retained dividing point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Accept a finite safeguarded proposal; otherwise bisect the current bracket. The midpoint is interior and permits a bracket update with at most half the former width.
assumptions_latex: \(0\leq a<b\) is a valid line-search bracket.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha\in[a+\delta(b-a),b-\delta(b-a)]\), with \(\alpha=(a+b)/2\) whenever the proposed trial is invalid or unsafe.

notation.meaning: Current lower and upper trial-step endpoints.

children.title: Line-Search Failure Recovery
children.top_down_role: Fallback regimes for rejected, invalid, or numerically unreliable trials.

knowledge_statements.title: Line-Search Failure Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite recovery protocol for rejected, undefined, or numerically unreliable line-search evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At iterate \(x_k\) with descent direction \(d_k\), retain the last finite bracket and an initial fallback step \(\alpha_{\mathrm{fb}}>0\). After an invalid evaluation or exhaustion of at most \(N\) ordinary trials, discard all nonfinite data and try \(\alpha_j=\alpha_{\mathrm{fb}}\rho^j\) for \(j=0,\ldots,R\), where \(\rho\in(0,1)\). Accept the first finite trial satisfying the prescribed sufficient-decrease test and set \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_jd_k\). If none is accepted, return \(x_k\) unchanged with failure status; do not update curvature or spectral information from rejected trials.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After ordinary search fails, retry finitely many geometrically reduced safe steps. Accept the first finite sufficient-decrease trial; otherwise keep the iterate and report failure.
assumptions_latex: \(f(x_k)\) and \(\nabla f(x_k)\) are finite, with \(\nabla f(x_k)^{\mathsf T}d_k<0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure either returns an accepted finite step or terminates after at most \(N+R+1\) trial evaluations with \(x_{k+1}=x_k\).

knowledge_statements.title: Long Spectral Steps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The first Barzilai–Borwein stepsize, conventionally the longer member of the BB pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For successive iterates of smooth unconstrained minimization, set \(s_{k-1}=x_k-x_{k-1}\) and \(y_{k-1}=
abla f(x_k)-
abla f(x_{k-1})\). When \(s_{k-1}^{\mathsf T}y_{k-1}>0\), the long spectral stepsize is
\[\alpha_k^{\mathrm{long}}=\alpha_k^{\mathrm{BB1}}= rac{s_{k-1}^{\mathsf T}s_{k-1}}{s_{k-1}^{\mathsf T}y_{k-1}}.\]
It is the least-squares scalar inverse-Hessian fit minimizing \(\lVert s_{k-1}-\alpha y_{k-1}Vert_2\) over \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\). The corresponding gradient step is \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_k^{\mathrm{long}}
abla f(x_k)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The long BB step divides squared displacement length by displacement–gradient-change curvature and is the scalar inverse-Hessian secant least-squares fit.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable at \(x_{k-1}\) and \(x_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha_k^{\mathrm{long}}=(s_{k-1}^{\mathsf T}s_{k-1})/(s_{k-1}^{\mathsf T}y_{k-1})>0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Short Spectral Steps

For \(s_{k-1}=x_k-x_{k-1}\) and \(y_{k-1}=

eq0\) and \(s_{k-1}^{\mathsf T}y_{k-1}>0\), the short spectral stepsize is

children.title: Long–Short Step Selection
children.top_down_role: Criteria for choosing between the canonical spectral branches.

knowledge_statements.title: Long–Short Step Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Curvature-ratio rule selecting between the two positive Barzilai–Borwein steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Compute positive candidates \(\alpha_k^{\mathrm{long}}\) and \(\alpha_k^{\mathrm{short}}\) from the current secant pair and fix \(\tau\in(0,1)\). Define \(r_k=\alpha_k^{\mathrm{short}}/\alpha_k^{\mathrm{long}}\). Select
\[\alpha_k=\begin{cases}\alpha_k^{\mathrm{short}},&r_k<\tau,\\ \alpha_k^{\mathrm{long}},&r_k\geq\tau.\end{cases}\]
Then take \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_k\nabla f(x_k)\), subject to any separate globalization safeguard. If either candidate is undefined or nonpositive, the selection rule is bypassed and a prescribed positive fallback is used.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compare the short-to-long BB ratio with a threshold: use the short step for a small ratio, otherwise the long step; invalid curvature triggers fallback.
assumptions_latex: Both BB candidates are finite and positive unless the stated fallback is invoked.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha_k\in\{\alpha_k^{\mathrm{long}},\alpha_k^{\mathrm{short}}\}\) when both candidates are valid, and otherwise \(\alpha_k>0\) is supplied by the fallback.

children.title: Alternating Spectral Steps

knowledge_statements.title: Alternating Spectral Steps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic iteration-by-iteration alternation of the two Barzilai–Borwein formulas.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Choose an offset \(q\in\{0,1\}\). At every \(k\geq1\), compute the valid long and short spectral candidates from \((s_{k-1},y_{k-1})\), and set
\[\alpha_k=\begin{cases}\alpha_k^{\mathrm{long}},&k+q\text{ is even},\\ \alpha_k^{\mathrm{short}},&k+q\text{ is odd}.\end{cases}\]
Apply any prescribed clipping to \(\alpha_k\), then update \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_k\nabla f(x_k)\). If the selected candidate is undefined or nonpositive, replace it by the designated positive fallback without changing the parity schedule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use the long and short BB formulas on alternating iterations, with optional clipping and a positive fallback for an invalid selected candidate.
assumptions_latex: The long and short candidate formulas are specified for each available secant pair.
\(q\in\{0,1\}\) fixes which formula is used first.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each valid candidate formula is selected on every second iteration according to the fixed parity offset.

knowledge_statements.title: Cyclic Spectral Steps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Periodic reuse of a spectral stepsize over fixed-length iteration blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a cycle length \(m\geq1\). At indices \(k=jm\), compute a valid safeguarded spectral value \(\widehat\alpha_j\) from the newest secant pair. For every \(i=0,\ldots,m-1\), set \(\alpha_{jm+i}=\widehat\alpha_j\) and update \(x_{jm+i+1}=x_{jm+i}-\alpha_{jm+i}\nabla f(x_{jm+i})\). If the cycle-start spectral formula is undefined or nonpositive, define \(\widehat\alpha_j\) by a prescribed positive fallback. Stop early when the algorithm's termination test holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compute one safeguarded spectral step at each cycle boundary and reuse it for a fixed number of gradient iterations.
assumptions_latex: Every cycle-start rule returns a finite positive value after safeguarding.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha_{jm}=\alpha_{jm+1}=\cdots=\alpha_{jm+m-1}=\widehat\alpha_j\) for every completed cycle \(j\).

children.title: Spectral Switching Schedules

knowledge_statements.title: Spectral Switching Schedules
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General history-dependent scheduling between finitely many safeguarded spectral formulas.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal A=\{A_1,\ldots,A_p\}\) be spectral candidate rules, let \(H_k\) contain information available through iteration \(k\), and let \(\sigma_k:H_k\to\{1,\ldots,p\}\) be a deterministic switching map. A spectral switching schedule generates \(\widehat\alpha_k=A_{\sigma_k(H_k)}(H_k)\), replaces an invalid value by a prescribed positive fallback, and optionally clips it to \([\alpha_{\min},\alpha_{\max}]\). The gradient update uses the resulting \(\alpha_k\). Alternating, cyclic, and curvature-ratio selections arise from parity-, block-, and secant-dependent choices of \(\sigma_k\), respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A switching schedule chooses among finitely many spectral formulas using only iteration history, then applies fallback and optional bounds before the gradient update.
assumptions_latex: \(1\leq p<\infty\), and each candidate rule uses only information in \(H_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The scheduled safeguarded step satisfies \(\alpha_k\in[\alpha_{\min},\alpha_{\max}]\) whenever clipping is enabled.

children.title: Spectral Gradient Interpretations

children.title: Scalar Secant-Metric View
children.top_down_role: Spectral scaling as a scalar variable-metric approximation.

knowledge_statements.title: Scalar Secant-Metric View
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Barzilai–Borwein scaling as least-squares scalar secant fitting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given nonzero secant data \(s=x_k-x_{k-1}\) and \(y=\nabla f(x_k)-\nabla f(x_{k-1})\), approximate the inverse Hessian by \(H=\alpha I\), or the Hessian by \(B=\beta I\). The least-squares secant fits are
\[\arg\min_{\alpha\in\mathbb R}\lVert s-\alpha y\rVert_2^2=\frac{s^{\mathsf T}y}{y^{\mathsf T}y},\qquad \left(\arg\min_{\beta\in\mathbb R}\lVert \beta s-y\rVert_2^2\right)^{-1}=\frac{s^{\mathsf T}s}{s^{\mathsf T}y},\]
provided the displayed denominators and reciprocal are defined. Thus the short and long BB steps are the two scalar variable-metric secant fits.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fitting either a scalar inverse Hessian or scalar Hessian to the secant equation yields, respectively, the short and long BB steps.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inverse-metric and metric least-squares fits produce \(\alpha^{\mathrm{BB2}}\) and \(\alpha^{\mathrm{BB1}}\), respectively.

children.title: Quadratic Spectral-Filter View
children.top_down_role: Eigendirection behavior of spectral steps on quadratic models.

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Spectral-Filter View
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact eigendirection action of scalar-step gradient descent on a positive-definite quadratic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx-b^{\mathsf T}x\), where \(Q=U\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n)U^{\mathsf T}\) is positive definite, and let \(x_*=Q^{-1}b\). For the scalar-step update \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_k\nabla f(x_k)\), the error \(e_k=x_k-x_*\) satisfies
\[U^{\mathsf T}e_{k+1}=\operatorname{diag}(1-\alpha_k\lambda_1,\ldots,1-\alpha_k\lambda_n)U^{\mathsf T}e_k.\]
Consequently, after \(k\) steps, eigendirection \(i\) is multiplied by the polynomial filter \(p_k(\lambda_i)=\prod_{j=0}^{k-1}(1-\alpha_j\lambda_i)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a positive-definite quadratic, each Hessian eigendirection is multiplied per step by one minus stepsize times eigenvalue, producing a polynomial spectral filter.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) is symmetric positive definite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((U^{\mathsf T}e_k)_i=p_k(\lambda_i)(U^{\mathsf T}e_0)_i\) with \(p_k(t)=\prod_{j=0}^{k-1}(1-\alpha_jt)\).

notation.meaning: Error relative to the unique minimizer.
Iteration polynomial acting on Hessian eigenvalues.

children.title: Spectral Stepsize Safeguards

knowledge_statements.title: Spectral Stepsize Safeguards
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Clipping and positive fallback for undefined or unreliable spectral curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(0<\alpha_{\min}\leq\alpha_{\max}<\infty\) and a fallback \(\alpha_{\mathrm{fb}}\in[\alpha_{\min},\alpha_{\max}]\). From secant data \((s,y)\), compute the chosen raw spectral value \(\widehat\alpha\) only if its denominator is safely nonzero and \(s^{\mathsf T}y>0\). If \(\widehat\alpha\) is finite and positive, set \(\alpha=\min\{\alpha_{\max},\max\{\alpha_{\min},\widehat\alpha\}\}\); otherwise set \(\alpha=\alpha_{\mathrm{fb}}\). Use \(\alpha\) for the trial gradient step, subject to any separate acceptance test.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use a finite positive spectral estimate only under reliable positive curvature, clip it to fixed bounds, and otherwise substitute a bounded positive fallback.

knowledge_statements.title: Indefinite or Vanishing Secant Curvature
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of unguarded Barzilai–Borwein quotients when secant curvature is nonpositive or negligible.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(s_k=x_k-x_{k-1}
eq 0\) and \(y_k=
abla f(x_k)-
abla f(x_{k-1})\). The BB1 and BB2 spectral steps are \[\alpha_k^{\mathrm{BB1}}= rac{s_k^{\mathsf T}s_k}{s_k^{\mathsf T}y_k},\qquad \alpha_k^{\mathrm{BB2}}= rac{s_k^{\mathsf T}y_k}{y_k^{\mathsf T}y_k}.\] If \(s_k^{\mathsf T}y_k\le 0\), neither quotient supplies a positive curvature-based step; BB1 is undefined when the denominator vanishes. If \(s_k^{\mathsf T}y_k>0\) but approaches zero relative to \(\lVert s_kVert^2\), then \(\alpha_k^{\mathrm{BB1}}\) becomes arbitrarily large. Consequently, an unguarded update can lose descent or numerical stability, motivating rejection, clipping, or safeguarded fallback steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonpositive secant curvature invalidates positive spectral scaling, while nearly zero curvature can make BB1 arbitrarily large; unguarded spectral updates may therefore lose descent or stability.

children.title: Spectral-Step Oscillation

knowledge_statements.title: Spectral-Step Oscillation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Alternation of BB spectral scales across directions with widely separated curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the quadratic \(f(x)=\tfrac12 x^{\mathsf T}Qx\), where \(Q\) is symmetric positive definite with eigenvalues in \([\mu,L]\), every nonzero secant \(s_k\) satisfies \[\alpha_k^{\mathrm{BB1}}=\frac{s_k^{\mathsf T}s_k}{s_k^{\mathsf T}Qs_k}\in\left[\frac1L,\frac1\mu\right].\] Secants dominated successively by high- and low-curvature eigenspaces produce spectral steps near \(1/L\) and \(1/\mu\), respectively. knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On ill-conditioned quadratics, changing secant directions can drive BB1 repeatedly between approximately 1/L and 1/μ, producing large step oscillations without monotone descent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha_k^{\mathrm{BB1}}\) may oscillate across the full interval \([1/L,1/\mu]\), whose endpoint ratio is \(L/\mu\).

abla f(x_k)\), define \(\Delta_0=f(x_0)-f_{\inf}\). For every integer \(N\ge 1\), \[\min_{0\le k<N}\lVert

abla f(x_k)\). Then \[\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\lVert

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stationarity of every finite cluster point when trajectory residuals vanish.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be continuously differentiable, and let \((x_k)_{k\ge0}\) satisfy \(\lVert\nabla f(x_k)\rVert\to0\). If a subsequence \((x_{k_j})_{j\ge0}\) converges to \(\bar x\in\mathbb R^n\), then \[\nabla f(\bar x)=0.\] Hence every cluster point of the trajectory is first-order stationary. children.title: Convex Objective-Gap Rates

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Objective-Gap Rates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Last-iterate objective rate for basic gradient descent on a smooth convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be convex with an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, and assume \(X^*:=\operatorname*{argmin}f\neq\varnothing\). For \(x_{k+1}=x_k-L^{-1}\nabla f(x_k)\), any \(x^*\in X^*\), and every integer \(N\ge1\), \[f(x_N)-f(x^*)\le \frac{L\lVert x_0-x^*\rVert^2}{2N}.\] Consequently, achieving objective gap at most \(\varepsilon>0\) requires no more than \(N\ge L\lVert x_0-x^*\rVert^2/(2\varepsilon)\) gradient steps, up to integer rounding; the rate is \(O(1/N)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For convex L-smooth minimization, gradient descent with step 1/L gives a last-iterate objective gap at most L times the initial squared distance divided by 2N.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex and has an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x_N)-f(x^*)\le L\lVert x_0-x^*\rVert^2/(2N)\), giving \(O(L\lVert x_0-x^*\rVert^2/\varepsilon)\) gradient complexity.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Gradient-Norm Rates

Let \(f:\mathbb R^n	o\mathbb R\) be convex with an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient and nonempty minimizer set. Under \(x_{k+1}=x_k-L^{-1}
abla f(x_k)\), for every minimizer \(x^*\) and integer \(N\ge1\), smooth convexity gives \(\lVert
abla f(x_N)Vert^2\le 2L(f(x_N)-f(x^*))\). Therefore \[\lVert

abla f(x_N)Vert\le\varepsilon\) is guaranteed once \(N\ge L^2\lVert x_0-x^*Vert^2/\varepsilon^2\), up to integer rounding.

knowledge_statements.title: Strongly Convex Gradient Rates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global linear objective and iterate rates for reciprocal-smoothness gradient descent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be \(\mu\)-strongly convex with an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, where \(0<\mu\le L\), and let \(x^*\) be its unique minimizer. For \(x_{k+1}=x_k-L^{-1}\nabla f(x_k)\), \[f(x_k)-f(x^*)\le \left(1-\frac{\mu}{L}\right)^k\bigl(f(x_0)-f(x^*)\bigr).\] Strong convexity then yields \[\lVert x_k-x^*\rVert^2\le \frac{2}{\mu}\left(1-\frac{\mu}{L}\right)^k\bigl(f(x_0)-f(x^*)\bigr).\] Thus reducing either displayed upper bound by a factor \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) takes \(O((L/\mu)\log(1/\varepsilon))\) gradient evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For μ-strongly convex, L-smooth objectives, step-1/L gradient descent contracts the objective geometrically with factor 1−μ/L and yields a corresponding geometric iterate-distance bound.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex and has an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The objective gap contracts by \((1-\mu/L)^k\), and the iteration complexity is \(O((L/\mu)\log(1/\varepsilon))\).

knowledge_statements.title: Polyak-Lojasiewicz Gradient-Descent Rates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global linear objective convergence under the Polyak–Łojasiewicz inequality, without convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) have an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, attain its finite minimum value \(f^*\), and satisfy the Polyak–Łojasiewicz inequality \[\frac12\lVert\nabla f(x)\rVert^2\ge \mu\bigl(f(x)-f^*\bigr)\qquad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb R^n\] for some \(\mu>0\). Gradient descent with \(x_{k+1}=x_k-L^{-1}\nabla f(x_k)\) obeys \[f(x_k)-f^*\le\left(1-\frac{\mu}{L}\right)^k\bigl(f(x_0)-f^*\bigr).\] Hence an objective gap at most \(\varepsilon>0\) is obtained within \(O((L/\mu)\log((f(x_0)-f^*)/\varepsilon))\) gradient evaluations. Convexity is not required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The PL inequality converts smooth descent into geometric objective convergence with factor 1−μ/L, even when the objective is nonconvex.

children.title: Local Error-Bound Rates
children.top_down_role: Eventual fast behavior in residual-controlled neighborhoods.

knowledge_statements.title: Local Error-Bound Rates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local linear convergence of fixed-step gradient descent under a gradient error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex and differentiable, with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient on a neighborhood \(U\) of the nonempty solution set \(X^*\). Suppose \(\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\leq\kappa\|\nabla f(x)\|\) for every \(x\in U\). For gradient descent \(x_{k+1}=x_k-L^{-1}\nabla f(x_k)\), if \(x_k\in U\) for all \(k\geq k_0\), then
\[
f(x_{k+1})-f^*\leq\left(1-\frac{1}{2L\kappa}\right)(f(x_k)-f^*)
\]
for every \(k\geq k_0\). Consequently, the objective errors converge locally at a linear rate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Once gradient descent remains in a neighborhood satisfying a gradient error bound, its objective error contracts by a fixed factor at every iteration.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex with an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient on \(U\).

knowledge_statements.title: Sufficient-Decrease Convergence Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Summability and stationarity consequences of uniformly quantified accepted decrease.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable and bounded below along iterates \((x_k)\). If accepted updates satisfy
\[
f(x_k)-f(x_{k+1})\geq c\|\nabla f(x_k)\|^2
\]
with a constant \(c>0\), then
\[
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\|\nabla f(x_k)\|^2\leq\frac{f(x_0)-\inf_j f(x_j)}{c}<\infty.
\]
Hence \(\|\nabla f(x_k)\|\to0\). This condition includes line-search schemes whose descent-angle, accepted-step, and Armijo bounds jointly yield a uniform value of \(c\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A uniform decrease proportional to the squared gradient makes squared residuals summable and forces gradients to vanish.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\|\nabla f(x_k)\|^2<\infty\) and \(\|\nabla f(x_k)\|\to0\).

children.top_down_role: Angle-and-curvature globalization framework for line-search directions.

children.title: Gradient-Direction Specialization
children.top_down_role: Consequences for steepest-descent directions.

knowledge_statements.title: Gradient-Direction Specialization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Zoutendijk summability specialized to the negative-gradient search direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuously differentiable, bounded below on the initial level set, and have a Lipschitz gradient on a neighborhood of that set. Consider \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kd_k\), where \(d_k=-\nabla f(x_k)\) and \(\alpha_k\) satisfies the Wolfe conditions with fixed \(0<c_1<c_2<1\). The Zoutendijk condition then specializes to
\[
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\|\nabla f(x_k)\|^2<\infty,
\]
because the angle cosine between \(-\nabla f(x_k)\) and \(d_k\) equals one. Therefore \(\|\nabla f(x_k)\|\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For Wolfe line search along the negative gradient, Zoutendijk summability directly implies convergence of the gradient norm to zero.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is bounded below on the initial level set and has a Lipschitz gradient nearby.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_k\|\nabla f(x_k)\|^2<\infty\), hence \(\|\nabla f(x_k)\|\to0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The steepest-descent specialization of Zoutendijk summability is mathematically standard and the theorem content kind fits the leaf, but no source or inspectable locator is supplied.

children.title: Nonlinear Conjugate-Gradient Specialization
children.top_down_role: Consequences for angle-controlled conjugate-gradient directions.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonlinear Conjugate-Gradient Specialization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Zoutendijk consequence for uniformly gradient-related nonlinear conjugate-gradient directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) satisfy the standard Zoutendijk hypotheses, and let \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kd_k\) use descent directions with Wolfe-accepted step lengths. Define
\[
\cos\theta_k=\frac{-\nabla f(x_k)^{\mathsf T}d_k}{\|\nabla f(x_k)\|\,\|d_k\|}.
\]
If nonlinear conjugate-gradient directions satisfy \(\cos\theta_k\geq\delta>0\) uniformly, then Zoutendijk summability gives
\[
\delta^2\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\|\nabla f(x_k)\|^2\leq\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\cos^2\theta_k\|\nabla f(x_k)\|^2<\infty.
\]
Consequently, \(\|\nabla f(x_k)\|\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Wolfe line search makes angle-controlled nonlinear conjugate-gradient directions globally stationary through Zoutendijk summability.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) satisfies the bounded-level-set and Lipschitz-gradient hypotheses of Zoutendijk's theorem.
\(d_k\) is a descent direction and \(\alpha_k\) satisfies Wolfe conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_k\|\nabla f(x_k)\|^2<\infty\) and \(\|\nabla f(x_k)\|\to0\).

notation.meaning: Angle between the negative gradient and search direction.
Uniform positive lower bound on the angle cosine.

children.title: Stopping Certificates
children.top_down_role: Computable residual and progress families used to terminate smooth unconstrained methods.

children.title: First-Order Residual Certificates
children.top_down_role: Gradient-based evidence of approximate stationarity.

knowledge_statements.title: First-Order Residual Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unconstrained approximate-stationarity certificate based on the gradient norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a differentiable objective \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), define the first-order residual by \(r(x)=\|\nabla f(x)\|\). Given a tolerance \(\varepsilon\geq0\), a computed point \(x\) satisfying
\[
r(x)\leq\varepsilon
\]
is an \(\varepsilon\)-first-order stationary point. The certificate is directly verifiable by evaluating the gradient and its norm. When \(\varepsilon=0\), it verifies the necessary first-order condition for an unconstrained local minimizer, but without convexity or additional geometry it does not certify local or global optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gradient norm at most the prescribed tolerance certifies approximate first-order stationarity, but not optimality in a general nonconvex problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|\nabla f(x)\|\leq\varepsilon\) certifies \(\varepsilon\)-first-order stationarity.

notation.meaning: First-order residual at the candidate point.

children.title: Progress-Stagnation Certificate System
children.top_down_role: Function, step, and directional evidence used to detect limited progress.

children.title: Objective-Progress Certificates
children.top_down_role: Function-value evidence indicating meaningful optimization progress.

knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Progress Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual inference from observed objective decrease and a quantified decrease inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose an accepted iteration satisfies
\[
0\leq f(x_k)-f(x_{k+1})\leq\tau_f
\quad\text{and}\quad
f(x_k)-f(x_{k+1})\geq c\|\nabla f(x_k)\|^2
\]
for known constants \(\tau_f\geq0\) and \(c>0\). Then the recorded objective values certify
\[
\|\nabla f(x_k)\|\leq\sqrt{\tau_f/c}.
\]
Without the lower sufficient-decrease inequality, the upper bound on objective change certifies only small observed progress; it is not by itself a stationarity certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Small objective decrease certifies a small gradient only when a known sufficient-decrease inequality links the two quantities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|\nabla f(x_k)\|\leq\sqrt{\tau_f/c}\).

children.title: Step-Progress Certificates
children.top_down_role: Displacement-based evidence indicating meaningful iterate movement.

knowledge_statements.title: Step-Progress Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gradient residual inferred from a small gradient step and a step-size lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a gradient update \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_k\nabla f(x_k)\), suppose the accepted step length satisfies \(\alpha_k\geq\underline{\alpha}>0\). If the computed displacement obeys
\[
\|x_{k+1}-x_k\|\leq\tau_x,
\]
then the update identity gives the verifiable certificate
\[
\|\nabla f(x_k)\|=\frac{\|x_{k+1}-x_k\|}{\alpha_k}
\leq\frac{\tau_x}{\underline{\alpha}}.
\]
Without a positive lower bound on \(\alpha_k\), a small displacement may merely reflect a vanishing step length and does not certify stationarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A small gradient-descent step certifies a small gradient only when the accepted step size is bounded away from zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|\nabla f(x_k)\|\leq\tau_x/\underline{\alpha}\).

notation.meaning: Known positive lower bound on accepted step lengths.

children.title: Directional-Progress Certificates
children.top_down_role: Directional evidence derived from local search behavior.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|\nabla f(x_k)\|\leq\sqrt{\tau_d/m}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stationarity inferred from small directional decrease and a gradient-related direction.

source_refs.source_title: Parallel and Distributed Computation: Numerical Methods

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(g_k=\nabla f(x_k)\), and suppose the search direction \(d_k\) is uniformly gradient-related in the sense that
\[
-g_k^{\mathsf T}d_k\geq m\|g_k\|^2
\]
for a known constant \(m>0\). If the computed directional progress satisfies
\[
0\leq -g_k^{\mathsf T}d_k\leq\tau_d,
\]
then it certifies
\[
\|\nabla f(x_k)\|\leq\sqrt{\tau_d/m}.
\]
Absent the gradient-related lower bound, near-orthogonality or poor scaling of \(d_k\) can make directional progress small while the gradient remains large.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Small directional decrease certifies approximate stationarity when the search direction has a known uniform relation to the gradient.

children.title: Stagnation Certificates
children.top_down_role: Evidence that further observed progress is negligible or numerically obscured.

knowledge_statements.title: Stagnation Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Windowed certificate of negligible recorded progress, conditional for stationarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a window length \(w\geq1\), tolerances \(\tau_f,\tau_x,\tau_d\geq0\), and indices \(j=k-w+1,\ldots,k\), the inequalities
\[
|f(x_{j+1})-f(x_j)|\leq\tau_f,
\quad \|x_{j+1}-x_j\|\leq\tau_x,
\quad |\nabla f(x_j)^{\mathsf T}d_j|\leq\tau_d
\]
form a verifiable windowed stagnation certificate. They certify that recorded objective, iterate, and directional changes all remain below tolerance throughout the window. They certify approximate stationarity only when an additional valid decrease, step-size, or gradient-relatedness inequality converts at least one observed tolerance into a first-order residual bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simultaneously small objective, step, and directional changes certify observed stagnation; stationarity requires an additional quantitative linkage to the gradient.
assumptions_latex: The three displayed progress tests hold for every \(j=k-w+1,\ldots,k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The iteration is stagnant over the stated window; no stationarity conclusion follows without a residual-linking inequality.

notation.meaning: Number of consecutive iterations in the monitoring window.
Objective, step, and directional stagnation tolerances.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record accurately distinguishes observed stagnation from stationarity and the certificate content kind fits the leaf. However, no source or inspectable locator supports this particular windowed certificate system or its validity qualification.

children.title: Geometry-Aware Accuracy Certificates
children.top_down_role: Stronger estimates available when target or curvature information is known.

children.title: Geometry-Aware Gap Certificates
children.top_down_role: Objective-suboptimality estimates supported by known target or curvature information.

knowledge_statements.title: Geometry-Aware Gap Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Frank–Wolfe gap certificate for differentiable convex optimization over a compact convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, compact, and convex, and let \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable and convex. For \(x\in C\), define the geometry-aware gap
\[
G_C(x)=\max_{y\in C}\langle\nabla f(x),x-y\rangle.
\]
If \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in C}f(y)\), convexity yields
\[
0\leq f(x)-f(x^*)\leq\langle\nabla f(x),x-x^*\rangle\leq G_C(x).
\]
Thus a computed value \(G_C(x)\leq\varepsilon\) certifies objective suboptimality at most \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Frank–Wolfe gap uses the feasible-set geometry and upper-bounds objective suboptimality for differentiable convex optimization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\leq f(x)-\min_{y\in C}f(y)\leq G_C(x)\).

notation.meaning: A minimizer of the constrained problem.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Frank-Wolfe gap bound is standard, but no source is supplied. A matching source should also state differentiability on an open neighborhood of C, or otherwise define the gradient at boundary points of C; writing only f:C to R is ambiguous there.

children.title: Geometry-Aware Distance Certificates
children.top_down_role: Solution-set proximity estimates supported by geometric information.

knowledge_statements.title: Geometry-Aware Distance Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distance-to-solution bound obtained from strong convexity and a feasible gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the geometry-aware gap setting, additionally suppose \(f\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex on \(C\), where \(\mu>0\). Then the constrained minimizer \(x^*\) is unique and
\[
\frac{\mu}{2}\|x-x^*\|^2\leq f(x)-f(x^*)\leq G_C(x).
\]
Consequently, a computed feasible gap satisfying \(G_C(x)\leq\varepsilon\) certifies
\[
\|x-x^*\|\leq\sqrt{\frac{2\varepsilon}{\mu}}.
\]
The certificate is geometry-aware because \(G_C(x)\) is obtained by optimizing the gradient linearization over the feasible set \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong convexity converts a feasible Frank–Wolfe gap into an explicit upper bound on distance to the unique optimizer.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable and \(\mu\)-strongly convex on \(C\), with \(\mu>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|x-x^*\|\leq\sqrt{2\varepsilon/\mu}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The strong-convexity conversion from a valid feasible gap to a distance bound is mathematically standard, but no source is supplied. As a standalone record it also relies on the preceding gap setting without explicitly defining G_C, requiring x in C, or declaring epsilon nonnegative.

children.title: Certificate Validity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Geometry classes determining when stronger gap or distance estimates are available.

knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Validity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp limitations of residual and progress-based stopping certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Stopping certificates retain only the conclusion justified by their structural assumptions. For \(f(x)=x\) and updates \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_k\) with \(\alpha_k\downarrow0\), both
\[
|x_{k+1}-x_k|=\alpha_k\to0
\quad\text{and}\quad
|f(x_{k+1})-f(x_k)|=\alpha_k\to0,
\]
while \(\|\nabla f(x_k)\|=1\); hence step and objective stagnation alone do not certify stationarity. Conversely, for \(f(x)=(x^2-1)^2\), the point \(x=0\) has \(\nabla f(0)=0\) but is not a local minimizer. Thus a zero first-order residual certifies stationarity, not optimality, without convexity or second-order information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vanishing steps or objective changes need not imply stationarity, and a zero gradient need not imply optimality in nonconvex problems.
assumptions_latex: The examples are unconstrained one-dimensional differentiable problems.
No step-size lower bound, sufficient-decrease linkage, convexity, or second-order condition is imposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Progress-only tests can fail to certify stationarity, and residual-only tests can fail to certify optimality.

notation.meaning: Vanishing prescribed step length in the first counterexample.

children.title: Smooth Convex Acceleration
children.top_down_role: Accelerated objective convergence in the smooth convex regime.

children.title: Classical Fast-Gradient Schemes
children.top_down_role: Canonical accelerated constructions for the convex smooth class.

knowledge_statements.title: Classical Fast-Gradient Schemes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unconstrained Euclidean Nesterov scheme for convex functions with Lipschitz-continuous gradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex with an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient and a minimizer \(x^*\). Initialize \(x_0=y_0\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(t_0=1\). For \(k\geq0\), compute
\[
x_{k+1}=y_k-L^{-1}\nabla f(y_k),\qquad t_{k+1}=\frac{1+\sqrt{1+4t_k^2}}{2},
\]
\[
y_{k+1}=x_{k+1}+\frac{t_k-1}{t_{k+1}}(x_{k+1}-x_k).
\]
After \(N\) gradient evaluations, output \(x_N\). The classical estimate is
\[
f(x_N)-f(x^*)\leq \frac{2L\lVert x_0-x^*\rVert^2}{(N+1)^2}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nesterov’s extrapolated gradient iteration uses one gradient per step and reduces smooth convex objective error at order inverse-square in the iteration count.
assumptions_latex: \(\lVert\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\rVert\leq L\lVert x-y\rVert\) for all \(x,y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x_N)-f(x^*)\leq 2L\lVert x_0-x^*\rVert^2/(N+1)^2\).

children.title: Accelerated Gradient-Norm Outputs
children.top_down_role: Accelerated constructions and output policies targeting first-order residuals.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is convex and has an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient.
For \(N\in\mathbb{N}\), the accelerated point \(z_N\) satisfies \(f(z_N)-f(x^*)\leq 2L\lVert x_0-x^*\rVert^2/(N+1)^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert\nabla f(x_{\mathrm{out}})\rVert\leq 2L\lVert x_0-x^*\rVert/(N+1)\), using \(N\) accelerated gradient evaluations and at most one additional gradient evaluation at the output point.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gradient-residual guarantee obtained by selecting an accelerated iterate and applying smooth convex self-bounding, with explicit output-gradient oracle accounting.

source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(N\in\mathbb{N}\). Under the smooth convex assumptions, suppose an accelerated method produces \(z_N\) satisfying
\[
f(z_N)-f(x^*)\leq \frac{2L\lVert x_0-x^*\rVert^2}{(N+1)^2}.
\]
Set \(x_{\mathrm{out}}=z_N\) and evaluate \(\nabla f(x_{\mathrm{out}})\). Smooth convex self-bounding gives
\[
\lVert\nabla f(x_{\mathrm{out}})\rVert^2\leq 2L\bigl(f(x_{\mathrm{out}})-f(x^*)\bigr),
\]
and therefore
\[
\lVert\nabla f(x_{\mathrm{out}})\rVert\leq \frac{2L\lVert x_0-x^*\rVert}{N+1}.
\]
Thus a gradient norm at most \(\varepsilon>0\) is obtained with \(N=O(L\lVert x_0-x^*\rVert/\varepsilon)\) accelerated steps and at most one additional first-order oracle call to evaluate the output gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An accelerated objective guarantee and smooth self-bounding give an inverse-linear gradient-norm bound at the accelerated output; evaluating that residual may require one additional gradient call.
