children.title: Strongly Convex Acceleration
children.top_down_role: Accelerated contraction in smooth strongly convex geometry.

children.title: Curvature-Calibrated Acceleration
children.top_down_role: Accelerated methods using known smoothness and strong-convexity scales.

knowledge_statements.title: Curvature-Calibrated Acceleration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constant-momentum accelerated gradient method calibrated by known smoothness and strong-convexity parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be \(L\)-smooth and \(\mu\)-strongly convex, where \(0<\mu\leq L\) are known. Set
\[
\beta=\frac{\sqrt L-\sqrt\mu}{\sqrt L+\sqrt\mu},
\]
initialize \(x_{-1}=x_0\), and for \(k\geq0\) compute
\[
y_k=x_k+\beta(x_k-x_{k-1}),\qquad x_{k+1}=y_k-L^{-1}\nabla f(y_k).
\]
Stop when a prescribed residual or iteration budget is met and output the latest \(x_k\). The stepsize and momentum depend only on the two curvature scales, and the associated convergence factor has accelerated dependence \(1-\Theta(\sqrt{\mu/L})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Known smoothness and strong-convexity constants determine a fixed gradient step and momentum whose contraction depends on the square root of the condition number.
assumptions_latex: The parameters \(L\) and \(\mu\) are available to the method.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The calibrated momentum is \(\beta=(\sqrt L-\sqrt\mu)/(\sqrt L+\sqrt\mu)\), giving accelerated condition-number dependence.

children.title: Restart-Based Strong-Convexity Adaptation
children.top_down_role: Recovery of fast contraction without directly embedding all curvature information.

knowledge_statements.title: Restart-Based Strong-Convexity Adaptation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Periodic restart of a convex accelerated method using strong convexity only to select the epoch length.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\) be \(L\)-smooth and \(\mu\)-strongly convex. Run a convex accelerated method for \(m\) steps from an epoch point \(u_s\), then restart its momentum at the resulting point \(u_{s+1}\). If its convex guarantee is
\[
f(u_{s+1})-f^*\leq \frac{2L\lVert u_s-x^*\rVert^2}{(m+1)^2},
\]
strong convexity yields
\[
f(u_{s+1})-f^*\leq\frac{4L}{\mu(m+1)^2}\bigl(f(u_s)-f^*\bigr).
\]
Choosing \(m+1\geq\sqrt{8L/\mu}\) halves the error each epoch, so \(O(\sqrt{L/\mu}\log((f(u_0)-f^*)/\varepsilon))\) gradient evaluations suffice.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restarting convex acceleration after a condition-number-scale epoch halves the objective error and recovers the accelerated strongly convex complexity.
assumptions_latex: Each epoch uses a convex accelerated method with the displayed objective guarantee.
Momentum is reset at every epoch boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The restarted method reaches \(f(u_s)-f^*\leq\varepsilon\) in \(O(\sqrt{L/\mu}\log((f(u_0)-f^*)/\varepsilon))\) gradient evaluations.

notation.meaning: starting point of restart epoch s
number of accelerated steps per epoch

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: follows by combining the classical accelerated convex bound with strong convexity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The restart complexity claim is standard and internally coherent, and complexity_bound fits the container, but no inspectable source is cited for the epoch construction or its constants.

children.title: Backtracking Acceleration
children.top_down_role: Accelerated methods with local smoothness search.

knowledge_statements.title: Backtracking Acceleration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Accelerated gradient with monotone local search for an acceptable quadratic upper-model curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x_0=y_0\), \(t_0=1\), an estimate \(M_0>0\), and growth factor \(\eta>1\), at iteration \(k\) choose the smallest \(M_k=M_{k-1}\eta^j\), with \(j\geq0\), for which \(x_{k+1}=y_k-M_k^{-1}\nabla f(y_k)\) satisfies
\[
f(x_{k+1})\leq f(y_k)+\langle\nabla f(y_k),x_{k+1}-y_k\rangle+\frac{M_k}{2}\lVert x_{k+1}-y_k\rVert^2.
\]
Then set
\[
t_{k+1}=\frac{1+\sqrt{1+4t_k^2}}2,\qquad y_{k+1}=x_{k+1}+\frac{t_k-1}{t_{k+1}}(x_{k+1}-x_k).
\]
Output the latest accepted iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each accelerated step enlarges a local curvature estimate until the smooth quadratic upper-model test accepts the trial gradient point.
assumptions_latex: \(\nabla f\) is globally Lipschitz, with unknown constant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every accepted step satisfies the displayed local quadratic upper-model inequality.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind and local quadratic acceptance test fit the leaf, but the first iteration refers to \(M_{k-1}\) at \(k=0\) despite initializing only \(M_0\). A source is also needed to fix and support the intended variable-curvature indexing.

children.title: Estimate-Sequence Framework
children.top_down_role: Nesterov's auxiliary-model framework for constructing accelerated guarantees.

children.title: Estimate-Function Models
children.top_down_role: Auxiliary lower-model families used by estimate sequences.

knowledge_statements.title: Estimate-Function Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex lower-model aggregation used to construct an estimate sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex and differentiable. Given query points \(y_i\), weights \(a_i>0\), and a convex seed \(\phi_0\), define \(A_k=\sum_{i=1}^k a_i\) and
\[
\phi_k(x)=\phi_0(x)+\sum_{i=1}^k a_i\bigl(f(y_i)+\langle\nabla f(y_i),x-y_i\rangle\bigr).
\]
Because every affine term is a global lower model of \(f\),
\[
\phi_k(x)\leq \phi_0(x)+A_k f(x)\qquad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb{R}^n.
\]
The minimizer and minimum of \(\phi_k\) provide the auxiliary model state used by estimate-sequence algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An estimate function adds weighted affine lower models of a convex objective to a convex seed, producing a globally controlled auxiliary model.
assumptions_latex: \(\phi_0\) is a proper convex seed function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\phi_k(x)\leq\phi_0(x)+A_k f(x)\) for all \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: affine first-order models globally minorize differentiable convex functions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Definition fits the estimate-function container and the displayed model inequality is standard. However, a merely proper convex seed need not make \(\phi_k\) attain a minimum, so the final minimizer claim needs stronger seed hypotheses or weaker wording, guided by an authoritative estimate-sequence source.

children.title: Estimate-Sequence Potentials
children.top_down_role: Weighted potential structures governing accelerated progress.

knowledge_statements.title: Estimate-Sequence Potentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical estimate-sequence inequality and its induced objective-error certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\lambda_k\geq0\) satisfy \(\lambda_k\to0\), and let functions \(\phi_k\) obey
\[
\phi_k(x)\leq(1-\lambda_k)f(x)+\lambda_k\phi_0(x)\qquad\text{for every }x.
\]
If an algorithm produces \(x_k\) such that \(f(x_k)\leq\inf_x\phi_k(x)\), then for every minimizer \(x^*\),
\[
f(x_k)-f(x^*)\leq\lambda_k\bigl(\phi_0(x^*)-f(x^*)\bigr).
\]
Consequently, selecting weights for which \(\lambda_k=O(k^{-2})\) yields the accelerated objective rate whenever the initial potential gap is finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An estimate sequence upper-controls its model minimum; comparing that minimum at an optimizer converts the decaying sequence weight into an objective-error bound.
assumptions_latex: The pair \((\phi_k,\lambda_k)\) satisfies the displayed estimate-sequence inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x_k)-f(x^*)\leq\lambda_k(\phi_0(x^*)-f(x^*))\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The estimate-sequence implication is internally consistent and property is an appropriate content kind, but the canonical definition and induced certificate have no inspectable source locator.

children.title: Coupling-Potential Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Acceleration interpreted through coupled progress mechanisms and Lyapunov functions.

children.title: Coupled-Progress Views
children.top_down_role: Interpretations based on interactions among complementary progress mechanisms.

knowledge_statements.title: Coupled-Progress Views
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Acceleration viewed as the weighted coupling of gradient and mirror-descent progress inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x^*\) minimize a convex differentiable function, let \(A_{k+1}=A_k+a_{k+1}\), and let \(D\) be a nonnegative Bregman divergence. A coupled accelerated step is certified when its gradient and mirror components combine to give
\[
a_{k+1}\bigl(f(y_{k+1})-f(x^*)\bigr)
\leq A_k\bigl(f(y_k)-f(y_{k+1})\bigr)+D(x^*,z_k)-D(x^*,z_{k+1}).
\]
Summing this inequality from \(k=0\) to \(N-1\) cancels the intermediate objective and divergence terms and yields
\[
A_N\bigl(f(y_N)-f(x^*)\bigr)\leq A_0\bigl(f(y_0)-f(x^*)\bigr)+D(x^*,z_0).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Acceleration follows when weighted gradient progress and mirror progress combine into a one-step inequality whose objective and divergence terms telescope.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex and differentiable with minimizer \(x^*\).
The iterates satisfy the displayed coupled-progress inequality.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: algebraic telescoping form of linear coupling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The one-step coupled-progress form and principle content kind match the leaf, but a specific linear-coupling source is needed to confirm the chosen states, weights, and Bregman-divergence orientation.

children.title: Potential-Function Views
children.top_down_role: Interpretations based on composite energy or Lyapunov quantities.

knowledge_statements.title: Potential-Function Views
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A weighted objective-plus-distance Lyapunov certificate for accelerated progress.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a minimizer \(x^*\), positive weights \(A_k\), objective iterates \(y_k\), and auxiliary states \(z_k\), define
\[
\Phi_k=A_k\bigl(f(y_k)-f(x^*)\bigr)+D(x^*,z_k),
\]
where \(D\) is a nonnegative Bregman divergence. If the algorithmic parameter conditions imply \(\Phi_{k+1}\leq\Phi_k\) for every \(k\), then
\[
f(y_N)-f(x^*)\leq\frac{\Phi_0}{A_N}.
\]
Thus the displayed potential is a verifiable convergence certificate: an accelerated choice \(A_N=\Theta(N^2)\) gives objective error \(O(N^{-2})\), provided \(\Phi_0<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonincreasing weighted objective-plus-distance potential certifies convergence; quadratic growth of its weight produces the inverse-square accelerated rate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(y_N)-f(x^*)\leq\Phi_0/A_N\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: immediate consequence of nonnegativity and potential monotonicity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Certificate is the correct mathematical role, and the conditional potential implication is sound. No source identifies the algorithmic parameter conditions under which the asserted monotonicity is obtained.

children.title: Coupling–Potential Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Connections between coupled-progress arguments and potential-based analyses.

knowledge_statements.title: Coupling–Potential Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic equivalence between a coupled one-step progress inequality and decrease of its associated potential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A_{k+1}=A_k+a_{k+1}\) and define
\[
\Phi_k=A_k\bigl(f(y_k)-f(x^*)\bigr)+D(x^*,z_k).
\]
Then the coupled-progress statement
\[
a_{k+1}\bigl(f(y_{k+1})-f(x^*)\bigr)
\leq A_k\bigl(f(y_k)-f(y_{k+1})\bigr)+D(x^*,z_k)-D(x^*,z_{k+1})
\]
is equivalent, by collecting the two objective terms using \(A_{k+1}=A_k+a_{k+1}\), to
\[
\Phi_{k+1}\leq\Phi_k.
\]
Hence the coupling proof and the potential proof encode the same one-step progress certificate under this identification of weights and states.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Collecting weighted objective terms converts the coupled gradient–mirror inequality exactly into monotonicity of the corresponding objective-plus-divergence potential.
assumptions_latex: The same iterates \(y_k,z_k\) and divergence \(D\) are used in both formulations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed coupled-progress inequality holds if and only if \(\Phi_{k+1}\leq\Phi_k\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct algebraic rearrangement of the two displayed formulations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Representation fits the correspondence leaf, and the two displayed formulations are algebraically equivalent under the stated identification. An inspectable source for this coupling-potential correspondence is still absent.

children.title: Polynomial Spectral-Filter Representation Pair
children.top_down_role: Quadratic-model interpretation of accelerated behavior across eigendirections.

children.title: Polynomial Iteration View
children.top_down_role: Quadratic-model behavior represented through iteration polynomials.

knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial Iteration View
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Accelerated linear iterations represented as residual polynomials on convex quadratic objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
f(x)=\tfrac12\langle x,Hx\rangle-\langle b,x\rangle,
\]
where \(H\) is symmetric positive definite, and let \(x^*=H^{-1}b\). For the constant-momentum iteration
\[
y_k=x_k+\beta(x_k-x_{k-1}),\qquad x_{k+1}=y_k-L^{-1}\nabla f(y_k),
\]
the errors \(e_k=x_k-x^*\) satisfy \(e_k=p_k(H)e_0\), with \(p_{-1}=p_0=1\) under \(x_{-1}=x_0\), and
\[
p_{k+1}(\lambda)=\left(1-\frac{\lambda}{L}\right)\bigl((1+\beta)p_k(\lambda)-\beta p_{k-1}(\lambda)\bigr).
\]
Thus convergence is governed mode-by-mode by the residual polynomial on the spectrum of \(H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a positive-definite quadratic, momentum errors equal a polynomial in the Hessian applied to the initial error, so each eigenmode follows a scalar recurrence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e_k=p_k(H)e_0\), with \(p_k\) satisfying the displayed scalar recurrence on each eigenvalue.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: substitution into the linear quadratic-gradient recurrence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The residual-polynomial recurrence is internally consistent for the stated quadratic iteration, and representation is the correct content kind. The record nevertheless lacks an authoritative polynomial-iteration or spectral-analysis locator.

children.title: Spectral-Filter View
children.top_down_role: Eigendirection attenuation interpreted through mode-dependent filtering.

knowledge_statements.title: Spectral-Filter View
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation of fixed-coefficient first-order iterations on symmetric positive-definite quadratics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f(x)=\tfrac12 x^{\mathsf T}Hx-b^{\mathsf T}x\), where \(H=U\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n)U^{\mathsf T}\succ0\), and let \(x_\star=H^{-1}b\). If a linear first-order method produces an error \(e_k=x_k-x_\star=p_k(H)e_0\) for a real polynomial \(p_k\) satisfying \(p_k(0)=1\), then
\[
e_k=U\operatorname{diag}\!\bigl(p_k(\lambda_1),\ldots,p_k(\lambda_n)\bigr)U^{\mathsf T}e_0.
\]
Thus the scalar response \(p_k(\lambda)\) is a spectral filter: each eigendirection of curvature \(\lambda_i\) is multiplied by \(p_k(\lambda_i)\), and convergence over a spectral set \(\Lambda\) follows from controlling \(\sup_{\lambda\in\Lambda}|p_k(\lambda)|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial first-order iteration acts independently on each Hessian eigenmode, multiplying the mode by the polynomial evaluated at its eigenvalue.
assumptions_latex: \(H\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) is symmetric positive definite.
The method has the polynomial error form \(e_k=p_k(H)e_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U^{\mathsf T}e_k=\operatorname{diag}(p_k(\lambda_i))U^{\mathsf T}e_0\).

notation.meaning: degree-at-most-k iteration polynomial or spectral response

children.title: Mode-Selective Acceleration
children.top_down_role: Differences in accelerated behavior across curvature modes.

knowledge_statements.title: Mode-Selective Acceleration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Acceleration interpreted through unequal attenuation of quadratic Hessian modes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the spectral-filter representation, write \(e_0=\sum_{i=1}^n c_i u_i\), where \(Hu_i=\lambda_i u_i\). Then
\[
\|e_k\|_2^2=\sum_{i=1}^n |c_i|^2|p_k(\lambda_i)|^2,
\qquad
\|e_k\|_H^2=\sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i|c_i|^2|p_k(\lambda_i)|^2.
\]
Consequently, relative to another iteration polynomial \(q_k\), the method is accelerated on a spectral subset \(S\) whenever \(|p_k(\lambda)|<|q_k(\lambda)|\) for \(\lambda\in S\). This improvement affects the realized error only through initial-error components whose eigenvalues lie in \(S\); it need not improve every mode or the worst-case response outside \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Acceleration can preferentially suppress selected curvature modes; its realized benefit depends on how the initial error is distributed across those modes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Mode \(i\) is attenuated by \(|p_k(\lambda_i)|\), weighted by its initial coefficient \(|c_i|\).

children.title: Quadratic Heavy-Ball Regime

children.title: Eigendirection Recurrence Analysis
children.top_down_role: Mode-by-mode organization of quadratic momentum dynamics.

knowledge_statements.title: Eigendirection Recurrence Analysis
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mode-by-mode form of heavy-ball dynamics on a strongly convex quadratic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Hx-b^{\mathsf T}x\) with \(H\succ0\), the heavy-ball iteration
\[
x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha(Hx_k-b)+\beta(x_k-x_{k-1})
\]
has error \(e_k=x_k-x_\star\). If \(Hu_i=\lambda_i u_i\) and \(z_{i,k}=u_i^{\mathsf T}e_k\), then every eigendirection evolves independently according to
\[
z_{i,k+1}=(1+\beta-\alpha\lambda_i)z_{i,k}-\beta z_{i,k-1}.
\]
Equivalently, \((z_{i,k+1},z_{i,k})^{\mathsf T}=A(\lambda_i)(z_{i,k},z_{i,k-1})^{\mathsf T}\), where \(A(\lambda)=\begin{pmatrix}1+\beta-\alpha\lambda&-\beta\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Diagonalizing the quadratic Hessian reduces heavy-ball dynamics to an independent scalar second-order recurrence for each curvature eigenvalue.
assumptions_latex: \(H\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) is symmetric positive definite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z_{i,k+1}=(1+\beta-\alpha\lambda_i)z_{i,k}-\beta z_{i,k-1}\) for every eigendirection \(i\).

notation.meaning: two-state transition matrix for curvature lambda

children.title: Quadratic Parameter Tuning
children.top_down_role: Momentum tuning relative to a known spectral interval.

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Parameter Tuning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimax heavy-ball tuning for a known positive spectral interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose the spectrum of the quadratic Hessian lies in \([m,L]\) with \(0<m\le L\). Among constant heavy-ball parameters, the classical minimax choice is
\[
\alpha_\star=\frac{4}{(\sqrt L+\sqrt m)^2},
\qquad
\beta_\star=\left(\frac{\sqrt L-\sqrt m}{\sqrt L+\sqrt m}\right)^2.
\]
For the characteristic polynomial \(r^2-(1+\beta_\star-\alpha_\star\lambda)r+\beta_\star\), every \(\lambda\in[m,L]\) has roots of modulus at most
\[
\rho_\star=\frac{\sqrt L-\sqrt m}{\sqrt L+\sqrt m}=\frac{\sqrt\kappa-1}{\sqrt\kappa+1},
\qquad \kappa=\frac Lm.
\]
The endpoint modes attain this bound, so the worst-mode asymptotic contraction factor equals \(\rho_\star\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Using the spectral endpoints gives the classical heavy-ball parameters and worst-mode contraction factor governed by the square root of the condition number.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is a quadratic with \(mI\preceq H\preceq LI\) and \(m>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_{\lambda\in[m,L]}\rho(A(\lambda))=\rho_\star=(\sqrt\kappa-1)/(\sqrt\kappa+1)\).

notation.meaning: lower and upper Hessian spectral bounds

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The classical parameter formulas and minimax spectral-radius claim are plausible and correctly scoped to strongly convex quadratics, but no inspectable source is cited for the minimax optimality assertion or endpoint attainment. An authoritative theorem, section, or page locator is required.

children.title: Nonquadratic Heavy-Ball Regimes
children.top_down_role: Heavy-ball behavior beyond exact quadratic models.

children.title: Smooth Convex Heavy-Ball
children.top_down_role: Global behavior in smooth convex geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Convex Heavy-Ball
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A conservative global convergence regime for constant-parameter heavy-ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be convex, bounded below, and differentiable with an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, and suppose \(\operatorname*{argmin}f\ne\varnothing\). For
\[
x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha\nabla f(x_k)+\beta(x_k-x_{k-1}),
\qquad 0\le\beta<1,
\qquad 0<\alpha<\frac{2(1-\beta)}L,
\]
define \(d_k=x_k-x_{k-1}\) and \(E_k=f(x_k)+\tfrac{\beta}{2\alpha}\|d_k\|^2\). Then \((E_k)\) is nonincreasing, \(\sum_k\|d_{k+1}\|^2<\infty\), and \(\nabla f(x_k)\to0\). If \((x_k)\) is bounded, every cluster point minimizes \(f\), and \(f(x_k)\to\min f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With a conservative step–momentum relation, a smooth convex heavy-ball trajectory has decreasing energy and approaches the minimizer set when bounded.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex, bounded below, and has an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient.
The minimizer set is nonempty and the generated iterates are bounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla f(x_k)\to0\), \(f(x_k)\to\min f\), and every cluster point belongs to \(\operatorname*{argmin}f\).

notation.meaning: heavy-ball energy combining objective and kinetic terms

source_refs.source_title: First-Order Methods in Optimization

source_witnesses.source_title: First-Order Methods in Optimization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated Lyapunov descent regime is mathematically plausible, but the cited section concerns smooth functions generally and does not establish the heavy-ball-specific convergence theorem. Because the record asserts a hypothesis-to-conclusion convergence result, theorem is a more exact content kind than property. A heavy-ball-specific authoritative locator is required before the statement and its boundary can be accepted.

children.title: Smooth Nonconvex Heavy-Ball
children.top_down_role: Stationarity and local behavior without convexity.

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Nonconvex Heavy-Ball
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Energy descent and first-order stationarity without convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be bounded below and continuously differentiable with an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient. For the constant-parameter heavy-ball iteration
\[
x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha\nabla f(x_k)+\beta(x_k-x_{k-1}),
\qquad 0\le\beta<1,
\qquad 0<\alpha<\frac{2(1-\beta)}L,
\]
set \(d_k=x_k-x_{k-1}\) and \(E_k=f(x_k)+\tfrac{\beta}{2\alpha}\|d_k\|^2\). Then \(E_k\) decreases, \(\sum_k\|d_{k+1}\|^2<\infty\), and \(\nabla f(x_k)\to0\). Hence every cluster point of a bounded trajectory is first-order stationary, although global optimality is not implied.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under a conservative parameter condition, nonconvex heavy-ball dissipates a kinetic energy and approaches first-order stationarity, not necessarily a global minimum.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is bounded below and has an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|x_{k+1}-x_k\|\to0\), \(\|\nabla f(x_k)\|\to0\), and each cluster point is stationary.

source_refs.source_title: First-Order Methods in Optimization

source_witnesses.source_title: First-Order Methods in Optimization

children.title: Heavy-Ball Stability

children.title: Characteristic-Root Stability
children.top_down_role: Quadratic recurrence stability through characteristic roots.

knowledge_statements.title: Characteristic-Root Stability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Schur stability condition for each quadratic heavy-ball mode.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a Hessian eigenvalue \(\lambda>0\), the heavy-ball error mode satisfies
\[
z_{k+1}=(1+\beta-\alpha\lambda)z_k-\beta z_{k-1}
\]
with characteristic polynomial \(\chi_\lambda(r)=r^2-(1+\beta-\alpha\lambda)r+\beta\). The mode converges to zero for every initial pair if and only if both roots lie in the open unit disk. For real \(\alpha>0\) and \(\beta\), the second-order Jury conditions reduce to
\[
-1<\beta<1,
\qquad
0<\alpha\lambda<2(1+\beta).
\]
Consequently, all modes of a quadratic with spectrum in \([m,L]\), where \(m>0\), are stable exactly when \(-1<\beta<1\) and \(0<\alpha L<2(1+\beta)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic heavy-ball mode is stable exactly when its two characteristic roots lie inside the unit disk, yielding explicit inequalities on step size and momentum.
assumptions_latex: The heavy-ball parameters are real and constant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho(A(\lambda))<1\iff -1<\beta<1\) and \(0<\alpha\lambda<2(1+\beta)\).

notation.meaning: characteristic polynomial of curvature mode lambda
spectral radius of transition matrix A

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The characteristic polynomial and reduced Jury inequalities are correctly stated for real constant parameters with positive step size, and condition is the appropriate content kind. No source with a specific locator is supplied for the necessary-and-sufficient stability criterion.

children.title: Momentum Stability Certificate System
children.top_down_role: Energy and robust-control certificates for momentum dynamics.

children.title: Lyapunov Stability Certificates
children.top_down_role: Energy-based stability assessment for momentum dynamics.

knowledge_statements.title: Lyapunov Stability Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic matrix certificate for uniform contraction of momentum states.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let the two-state error dynamics for curvature \(\lambda\in[m,L]\) be \(s_{k+1}=A(\lambda)s_k\). Fix \(0<\rho<1\). A symmetric matrix \(P\succ0\) satisfying
\[
A(\lambda)^{\mathsf T}PA(\lambda)\preceq\rho^2P
\qquad\text{for every }\lambda\in[m,L]
\]
is a uniform Lyapunov stability certificate. The computable scalar \(V(s)=s^{\mathsf T}Ps\) then satisfies \(V(s_k)\le\rho^{2k}V(s_0)\) for every admissible curvature sequence when the displayed inequality holds pointwise. For a fixed quadratic Hessian, applying the certificate to each eigendirection establishes linear convergence of the full heavy-ball state in the norm induced by \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A common positive-definite quadratic form certifies uniform linear stability when every admissible momentum transition contracts that form.
assumptions_latex: \(A(\lambda)\) is the heavy-ball state matrix for \(\lambda\in[m,L]\).
There exist \(P=P^{\mathsf T}\succ0\) and \(0<\rho<1\) satisfying the matrix inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V(s_k)\le\rho^{2k}V(s_0)\) for \(V(s)=s^{\mathsf T}Ps\).

notation.meaning: stacked current and previous modal errors

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The common quadratic matrix inequality is a valid certificate form and the certificate content kind fits the leaf. However, the extension from fixed quadratic modes to every admissible curvature sequence is a switched-system claim requiring authoritative support and an explicit source locator.

children.title: Integral-Quadratic-Constraint Certificates
children.top_down_role: Robust-control stability assessment using sector-based oracle descriptions.

knowledge_statements.title: Integral-Quadratic-Constraint Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: LMI certificate for momentum feedback with a sector-bounded gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Represent a momentum method as \(\xi_{k+1}=A\xi_k+Bu_k\), \(y_k=C\xi_k\), and \(u_k=\nabla f(y_k)\), translated so the equilibrium is zero. For an \(m\)-strongly convex, \(L\)-smooth gradient, the pointwise sector IQC is
\[
\begin{pmatrix}y_k\\u_k\end{pmatrix}^{\mathsf T}
Q
\begin{pmatrix}y_k\\u_k\end{pmatrix}\ge0,
\quad
Q=\begin{pmatrix}-2mL&m+L\\m+L&-2\end{pmatrix}\otimes I.
\]
Let \(T=\begin{pmatrix}C&0\\0&I\end{pmatrix}\). If \(P\succ0\), \(\tau\ge0\), and \(0<\rho<1\) satisfy
\[
\begin{pmatrix}A&B\end{pmatrix}^{\mathsf T}P\begin{pmatrix}A&B\end{pmatrix}-\rho^2\begin{pmatrix}I&0\end{pmatrix}^{\mathsf T}P\begin{pmatrix}I&0\end{pmatrix}+\tau T^{\mathsf T}QT\preceq0,
\]
then \(\xi_k^{\mathsf T}P\xi_k\le\rho^{2k}\xi_0^{\mathsf T}P\xi_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sector inequality for the gradient combined with a feasible matrix inequality certifies a linear contraction rate for momentum dynamics.
assumptions_latex: The momentum method admits the stated linear-feedback representation.
The displayed LMI is feasible with \(P\succ0\), \(\tau\ge0\), and \(0<\rho<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\xi_k^{\mathsf T}P\xi_k\le\rho^{2k}\xi_0^{\mathsf T}P\xi_0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record has the correct certificate role and gives a dimensionally coherent pointwise sector-IQC LMI under its stated feedback convention. Because IQC signs and interconnection conventions are convention-sensitive, the formula and contraction conclusion require an authoritative optimization-IQC source with a precise theorem or section locator.

children.title: Robust Momentum Stability Regions

knowledge_statements.title: Robust Momentum Stability Regions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameter region certified uniformly over a prescribed curvature uncertainty set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix \(0<m\le L\) and a desired rate \(0<\rho<1\). For a momentum state matrix \(A_{\alpha,\beta}(\lambda)\), define the common-quadratic robust stability region by
\[
\mathcal R_{m,L}(\rho)=\left\{(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathbb R^2:\ \exists P=P^{\mathsf T}\succ0\ \text{such that}\ A_{\alpha,\beta}(\lambda)^{\mathsf T}PA_{\alpha,\beta}(\lambda)\preceq\rho^2P\ \forall\lambda\in[m,L]\right\}.
\]
Membership certifies contraction with the same Lyapunov function for every admissible curvature. The rate-free region is \(\mathcal R_{m,L}=\bigcup_{0<\rho<1}\mathcal R_{m,L}(\rho)\). This common-certificate region may be smaller than the set obtained by checking characteristic roots separately for each fixed \(\lambda\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The robust stability region contains exactly those momentum parameters admitting one quadratic contraction certificate for every curvature in the uncertainty interval.
assumptions_latex: \(0<m\le L\) specifies the curvature uncertainty interval.
\(A_{\alpha,\beta}(\lambda)\) is the selected momentum state realization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\alpha,\beta)\in\mathcal R_{m,L}(\rho)\) exactly when a common quadratic \(\rho\)-contraction certificate exists.

notation.meaning: momentum transition matrix at curvature lambda

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed set is a coherent definition of a common-quadratic robust stability region, and definition is appropriate for this leaf. The additional comparison with modewise characteristic-root stability is a nontrivial claim, and no inspectable robust-control or optimization source is provided.

children.title: Momentum Oscillation
children.top_down_role: Persistent or slowly damped alternation caused by aggressive momentum.

knowledge_statements.title: Momentum Oscillation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Underdamped oscillation boundary for a scalar quadratic heavy-ball mode.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a quadratic eigenmode with curvature \(\lambda>0\) and momentum \(\beta>0\), the characteristic roots are nonreal exactly when
\[
(1+\beta-\alpha\lambda)^2<4\beta,
\quad\text{equivalently}\quad
(1-\sqrt\beta)^2<\alpha\lambda<(1+\sqrt\beta)^2.
\]
In this underdamped regime the roots are \(r_{\pm}=\sqrt\beta\,e^{\pm i\theta}\), where
\[
\cos\theta=\frac{1+\beta-\alpha\lambda}{2\sqrt\beta}.
\]
Every real solution has the form \(z_k=(\sqrt\beta)^k(a\cos(k\theta)+b\sin(k\theta))\). Thus \(0<\beta<1\) yields decaying oscillations, \(\beta=1\) yields undamped oscillations, and \(\beta>1\) yields oscillations with growing envelope.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complex characteristic roots produce oscillatory momentum modes whose envelope decays, persists, or grows according to whether momentum is below, equal to, or above one.
assumptions_latex: The scalar mode follows the constant-parameter heavy-ball recurrence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Oscillation occurs iff \((1-\sqrt\beta)^2<\alpha\lambda<(1+\sqrt\beta)^2\), with envelope \((\sqrt\beta)^k\).

notation.meaning: angular frequency of the conjugate characteristic roots

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: discriminant classification of characteristic roots

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The discriminant boundary, conjugate-root parameterization, and envelope classification are mathematically consistent and fit the failure-boundary container. An authoritative source with a section, theorem, or page locator is nevertheless required.

children.title: Momentum Overshoot
children.top_down_role: Transient passage beyond favorable regions or target levels.

knowledge_statements.title: Momentum Overshoot
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A concrete sign-crossing boundary for a quadratic heavy-ball trajectory.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider \(f(x)=\tfrac12\lambda x^2\) with \(\lambda>0\), minimizer \(x_\star=0\), and heavy-ball initialization \(x_{-1}=x_0>0\). The first update is
\[
x_1=(1-\alpha\lambda)x_0.
\]
Therefore \(\alpha\lambda>1\) causes immediate overshoot across the minimizer, while \(\alpha\lambda=1\) lands exactly at the minimizer on the first step. More generally, for any modal error sequence \((z_k)\), overshoot at iteration \(k+1\) is certified by \(z_kz_{k+1}<0\). Immediate overshoot can occur inside the asymptotically stable region \(0<\alpha\lambda<2(1+\beta)\); asymptotic stability therefore does not imply a monotone or nonovershooting trajectory.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even stable heavy-ball parameters can cross the minimizer; with zero initial velocity, the first step overshoots exactly when the scaled step exceeds one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_0x_1<0\iff\alpha\lambda>1\), and this is compatible with characteristic-root stability.

notation.meaning: dimensionless step size for the quadratic mode

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct evaluation of the first quadratic update

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The first-step sign-crossing condition is correct for zero initial velocity, and the statement appropriately distinguishes overshoot from asymptotic stability. The failure-boundary content kind fits, but no inspectable source is supplied for the overshoot characterization or its relation to the stable region.

children.title: Underdamped Parameter Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Underdamped Parameter Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar quadratic eigenmode definition for heavy-ball momentum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the heavy-ball iteration on \(f(x)=\tfrac12\lambda x^2\), define \(e_k=x_k\) and \(a=1+\beta-\alpha\lambda\). The error satisfies \(e_{k+1}=a e_k-\beta e_{k-1}\), with characteristic polynomial \(p(r)=r^2-ar+\beta\). The eigenmode is underdamped precisely when \(\beta>0\) and \[a^2-4\beta<0.\] Equivalently, \(1+\beta-2\sqrt{\beta}<\alpha\lambda<1+\beta+2\sqrt{\beta}\). Its roots are a complex-conjugate pair of modulus \(\sqrt{\beta}\); hence the underdamped mode is asymptotically stable when additionally \(0<\beta<1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A heavy-ball quadratic mode is underdamped when its characteristic roots are complex. Stable underdamped oscillations decay geometrically with root modulus equal to the square root of momentum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((1+\beta-\alpha\lambda)^2<4\beta\), with stable root modulus \(\sqrt{\beta}<1\).

children.title: Quadratic-Tuning Mismatch
children.top_down_role: Loss of predicted behavior under changing or nonquadratic curvature.

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic-Tuning Mismatch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of fixed-spectrum heavy-ball tuning under changing curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Quadratic tuning analyzes each fixed eigenvalue \(\lambda\) through one stationary recurrence matrix \[T(\lambda)=\begin{pmatrix}1+\beta-\alpha\lambda&-\beta\\1&0\end{pmatrix}.\] For a nonquadratic twice-differentiable objective, the mean-value Hessian along successive steps can produce matrices \(T(\lambda_k)\) with changing \(\lambda_k\). Bounds obtained solely from \(\max_{\lambda\in[m,L]}\rho(T(\lambda))\) do not control products \(T(\lambda_{k-1})\cdots T(\lambda_0)\), because individually stable matrices need not have uniformly stable products. Thus quadratic-optimal parameters require an additional common contraction or Lyapunov argument before their predicted rate can be transferred to varying curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rates tuned from fixed quadratic eigenmodes need not survive changing curvature, because convergence then depends on products of different recurrence matrices rather than their separate spectral radii.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is twice differentiable with curvature values in \([m,L]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Quadratic spectral-radius tuning alone does not imply the same rate for varying curvature.

notation.meaning: heavy-ball state-transition matrix at curvature lambda

children.title: Scheduled Restart
children.top_down_role: Periodic restart tied to known or estimated conditioning.

knowledge_statements.title: Scheduled Restart
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Periodic momentum reset for accelerated gradient descent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given differentiable \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\), smoothness estimate \(L>0\), momentum \(\beta_k\), restart period \(T\in\mathbb N\), and \(x_{-1}=x_0\), repeat for \(k=0,\ldots,N-1\): if \(k>0\) and \(k\equiv0\pmod T\), first set \(x_{k-1}=x_k\); then compute \[y_k=x_k+\beta_k(x_k-x_{k-1}),\qquad x_{k+1}=y_k-L^{-1}\nabla f(y_k).\] A reset therefore makes the extrapolation term zero at the scheduled iteration. Return \(x_N\), or stop earlier when a prescribed stationarity or accuracy test is met. The period may be fixed from known conditioning or an external condition-number estimate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Run accelerated gradient steps but erase momentum every fixed number of iterations. The period can be selected from known or estimated conditioning.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable and has an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm outputs \(x_N\) after momentum resets at multiples of \(T\).

children.title: Adaptive Restart
children.top_down_role: Function-based, gradient-based, and potential-based restart triggers.

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Restart
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Observable-triggered reset of accelerated-gradient momentum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) have an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient. Initialize \(x_0\in\mathbb R^n\) and a stored inertial displacement \(s_0=0\). At iteration \(k\), form \(y_k=x_k+\beta_k s_k\) and \(z_k=y_k-L^{-1}\nabla f(y_k)\), and evaluate a fully specified computable restart predicate \(R_k\), which may use function values, gradient-alignment data, or a specified potential \(\Phi_k\). If \(R_k\) is false, set \[x_{k+1}=z_k,\qquad s_{k+1}=x_{k+1}-x_k.\] If \(R_k\) is true, erase the inertial state and take the non-extrapolated step \[x_{k+1}=x_k-L^{-1}\nabla f(x_k),\qquad s_{k+1}=0.\] Stop by a prescribed accuracy test and return the latest accepted point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adaptive restart evaluates a specified function-based, gradient-based, or potential-based trigger. When it fires, the method takes a non-extrapolated gradient step and resets the stored inertial displacement to zero.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable with an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient.
Each restart predicate \(R_k\) is fully specified and computable from available iteration data.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Whenever \(R_k\) holds, the algorithm sets \(s_{k+1}=0\), so the next extrapolation has no inherited inertial displacement.

notation.meaning: a specified computable potential when a potential-based trigger is used

children.title: Momentum Noise Amplification
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity of inertial state to persistent oracle perturbations.

knowledge_statements.title: Momentum Noise Amplification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Input-output representation for persistent errors in one quadratic mode.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the perturbed heavy-ball iteration on \(f(x)=\tfrac12\lambda x^2\), let the gradient oracle return \(\lambda x_k+\xi_k\). With \(a=1+\beta-\alpha\lambda\), the error obeys \[e_{k+1}=a e_k-\beta e_{k-1}-\alpha\xi_k.\] Under zero initial state, its transfer function from oracle error to iterate error is \[H(z)=\frac{E(z)}{\Xi(z)}=\frac{-\alpha z}{z^2-a z+\beta}.\] If both characteristic roots lie inside the unit disk, the recurrence is bounded-input bounded-output stable, but its worst sinusoidal amplification is \(\sup_{|z|=1}|H(z)|\), which becomes large when a pole approaches the unit circle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Momentum filters oracle errors through a second-order recurrence. Stable parameters can still strongly amplify persistent errors when the recurrence poles lie near the unit circle.
assumptions_latex: \(\lambda>0\), \(\alpha>0\), and the oracle errors are additive.
The transfer-function statement uses zero initial state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E(z)/\Xi(z)=-\alpha z/(z^2-(1+\beta-\alpha\lambda)z+\beta)\).

notation.meaning: scalar error in the quadratic mode

children.title: Curvature-Parameter Misspecification

knowledge_statements.title: Curvature-Parameter Misspecification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact scalar stability boundary under an incorrect curvature scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a scalar quadratic mode of curvature \(\lambda>0\), heavy-ball with fixed parameters has characteristic polynomial \(r^2-(1+\beta-\alpha\lambda)r+\beta\). Its roots are strictly inside the unit disk exactly when \[|\beta|<1,\qquad 0<\alpha\lambda<2(1+\beta).\] Consequently, parameters selected using a curvature estimate \(\widehat L\) can become unstable on an actual mode \(\lambda\) whenever \(\alpha\lambda\ge2(1+\beta)\), even if \(\alpha\widehat L<2(1+\beta)\). Overestimating curvature may instead preserve stability while reducing the effective step and forfeiting the tuned acceleration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Heavy-ball stability depends on the true curvature, not the estimated one. Underestimating maximum curvature can cross the exact stability boundary; conservative overestimation can sacrifice speed.
assumptions_latex: The objective mode is \(f(x)=\tfrac12\lambda x^2\) with \(\lambda>0\).
Heavy-ball uses constant real parameters \(\alpha>0\) and \(\beta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strict stability holds if and only if \(|\beta|<1\) and \(0<\alpha\lambda<2(1+\beta)\).

children.title: Long Momentum Transients
children.top_down_role: Extended startup phases that delay practical acceleration gains.

knowledge_statements.title: Long Momentum Transients
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomially weighted decay near a repeated momentum root.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a homogeneous scalar momentum recurrence \(e_{k+1}=a e_k-\beta e_{k-1}\). If its characteristic polynomial has a repeated root \(r\), so that \(a=2r\) and \(\beta=r^2\), then every solution has the form \[e_k=(c_1+c_2k)r^k.\] Thus \(|r|<1\) ensures asymptotic convergence, yet the factor \(k\) can cause a long transient before geometric decay dominates. More generally, two distinct but nearly coincident roots make the modal decomposition ill-conditioned, permitting a large finite-time response even when both roots are strictly within the unit disk.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A repeated or nearly repeated stable momentum root produces polynomially weighted geometric decay. Iterates may therefore exhibit a long transient despite eventual convergence.
assumptions_latex: The recurrence has constant real coefficients.
For the displayed representation, the characteristic root \(r\) has algebraic multiplicity two.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e_k=(c_1+c_2k)r^k\), so stability does not preclude a long finite-time transient.

notation.meaning: constants fixed by the initial state

children.title: Finite-Precision Momentum Drift
children.top_down_role: Accumulation and persistence of arithmetic error in momentum state.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Precision Momentum Drift
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Accumulated roundoff represented as forced momentum dynamics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Model a computed scalar momentum mode by \(\widehat e_{k+1}=a\widehat e_k-\beta\widehat e_{k-1}+\delta_k\), where \(\delta_k\) is the aggregate local floating-point perturbation. Let \(h_{-1}=0\), \(h_0=1\), and \(h_{j+1}=a h_j-\beta h_{j-1}\). Relative to the exact recurrence with identical initial data, the drift is exactly \[\widehat e_k-e_k=\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}h_{k-1-i}\delta_i.\] Hence finite-precision effects are accumulated according to the same impulse response that governs momentum transients; small local errors need not remain small when \(\sum_j|h_j|\) is large.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Roundoff acts as a forcing term in the momentum recurrence. The resulting drift is the convolution of local errors with the method's impulse response.
assumptions_latex: Each computed update is representable as the exact recurrence plus an additive local error \(\delta_k\).
The computed and exact recurrences start from identical initial states.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat e_k-e_k=\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}h_{k-1-i}\delta_i\).

notation.meaning: impulse-response sequence of the momentum recurrence

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: variation-of-constants formula for a forced linear recurrence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The convolution identity is correct for an assumed additive forced recurrence, but no inspectable source supports interpreting aggregate floating-point effects through this model or its stated numerical implication.

children.title: Transient–Drift Interaction
children.top_down_role: Regimes where prolonged dynamics amplify or conceal finite-precision effects.

knowledge_statements.title: Transient–Drift Interaction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Roundoff amplification by repeated-root momentum transients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the forced repeated-root recurrence \[e_{k+1}=2r e_k-r^2e_{k-1}+\delta_k,\qquad |r|<1,\] the impulse response is \(h_j=(j+1)r^j\). Consequently, perturbation-induced drift satisfies \[d_k=\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}(k-i)r^{k-1-i}\delta_i.\] If \(|\delta_i|\le\varepsilon\), then \(|d_k|\le\varepsilon\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}(j+1)|r|^j\le\varepsilon(1-|r|)^{-2}\). Thus a stable but slowly decaying repeated root can amplify persistent numerical drift quadratically in the inverse stability margin, coupling long transients to finite-precision sensitivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a repeated stable root, the same polynomial factor causing long transients also amplifies accumulated perturbations, with a worst-case bound proportional to the inverse squared stability margin.
assumptions_latex: The drift recurrence has zero initial state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|d_k|\le\varepsilon(1-|r|)^{-2}\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: convolution bound for a repeated-root forced recurrence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The repeated-root impulse response and convolution bound are mathematically correct, but the record has no inspectable source supporting its finite-precision interpretation and inverse-stability-margin amplification claim.

knowledge_statements.title: Problem Equilibration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diagonal change of variables balancing coordinatewise curvature before fixed-metric gradient iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a differentiable objective \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), choose a nonsingular diagonal matrix \(D=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_n)\) with \(d_i>0\), set \(x=Dz\), and define \(\widetilde f(z)=f(Dz)\). Select \(D\) so that estimated coordinate curvature scales \(c_i>0\) satisfy \(d_i^2c_i\approx 1\), for example \(d_i=c_i^{-1/2}\). Apply gradient descent to \(\widetilde f\): \(z_{k+1}=z_k-\alpha_kD^{\mathsf T}\nabla f(Dz_k)\), and return \(x_k=Dz_k\). Equivalently, \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_kDD^{\mathsf T}\nabla f(x_k)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rescale variables to balance estimated coordinate curvatures, run gradient descent in the scaled variables, and map iterates back; this is equivalent to fixed diagonal preconditioning.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_kDD^{\mathsf T}\nabla f(x_k)\).

notation.meaning: estimated curvature scale of coordinate i

children.title: Scaling Quality Diagnostics

knowledge_statements.title: Scaling Quality Diagnostics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spectral and coordinatewise tests for whether a fixed scaling improves smooth-problem geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For twice differentiable \(f\) and nonsingular scaling \(D\), define the scaled Hessian \(H_D(x)=D^{\mathsf T}\nabla^2f(x)D\). On a region \(\Omega\), a scaling-quality certificate consists of constants \(0<\mu_D\le L_D<\infty\) satisfying \(\mu_DI\preceq H_D(x)\preceq L_DI\) for every \(x\in\Omega\). Its spectral diagnostic is \(\kappa_D=L_D/\mu_D\); smaller \(\kappa_D\) predicts a better worst-case linear rate for gradient descent on strongly convex objectives. Coordinate balance may additionally be checked through the spread of \((H_D(x))_{ii}\). These diagnostics are meaningful only relative to the unscaled values or competing scalings on the same region.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Certify scaling quality by bounding the scaled Hessian, comparing its condition number with alternatives, and checking whether its diagonal curvature scales are balanced.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is twice differentiable on a region \(\Omega\).
The scaled Hessian is uniformly positive definite on \(\Omega\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\kappa_D=L_D/\mu_D\), with smaller \(\kappa_D\) indicating better-conditioned scaled geometry.

notation.meaning: uniform upper and lower scaled-curvature bounds

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded Metric Sequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform spectral control and bounded relative variation for variable metrics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A sequence of symmetric matrices \((M_k)_{k\ge0}\) is uniformly bounded and coercive if constants \(0<m\le M<\infty\) exist such that \(mI\preceq M_k\preceq MI\) for every \(k\). A common stronger variable-metric condition requires a summable nonnegative sequence \((\eta_k)\) with \(M_{k+1}\preceq(1+\eta_k)M_k\) and \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\eta_k<\infty\). The first condition makes all induced norms uniformly equivalent to the Euclidean norm; the second prevents persistent multiplicative oscillation of the geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Variable metrics are stable when their eigenvalues stay uniformly away from zero and infinity, with optional summable control of successive metric changes.
assumptions_latex: The matrices act on a fixed finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sqrt m\lVert v\rVert_2\le\lVert v\rVert_{M_k}\le\sqrt M\lVert v\rVert_2\) for all \(v\) and \(k\).

notation.meaning: metric norm defined by the quadratic form

children.title: Diagonal Curvature Surrogates
children.top_down_role: Low-cost coordinatewise approximations of local curvature.

knowledge_statements.title: Diagonal Curvature Surrogates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Safeguarded diagonal approximations to local curvature for inexpensive variable-metric steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At iterate \(x_k\), construct positive coordinate curvature estimates \(c_{k,i}\), for example from diagonal Hessian information or secant ratios when available. Given safeguards \(0<\ell\le u<\infty\), set \(h_{k,i}=\min\{u,\max\{\ell,c_{k,i}\}\}\) and \(H_k=\operatorname{diag}(h_{k,1},\ldots,h_{k,n})\). The unconstrained variable-metric step is \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_kH_k^{-1}\nabla f(x_k)\). Thus each gradient component is divided by a local curvature surrogate while clipping ensures \(\ell I\preceq H_k\preceq uI\). Stop when a prescribed stationarity test is satisfied and return the last iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Estimate curvature separately by coordinate, clip the estimates to positive bounds, and divide each gradient component by its safeguarded estimate.
assumptions_latex: The raw curvature estimates \(c_{k,i}\) are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_kH_k^{-1}\nabla f(x_k)\) and \(\ell I\preceq H_k\preceq uI\).

children.title: Metric-Projection Interface
children.top_down_role: The constrained extension of variable-metric gradient steps.

knowledge_statements.title: Metric-Projection Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constrained variable-metric gradient step as a weighted projection or quadratic subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(M_k\succ0\). Given \(x_k\in C\) and \(\alpha_k>0\), compute \(y_k=x_k-\alpha_kM_k^{-1}\nabla f(x_k)\) and set \(x_{k+1}=P_C^{M_k}(y_k)\), where \(P_C^{M}(y)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\tfrac12\lVert x-y\rVert_M^2\). Equivalently, \(x_{k+1}\) uniquely minimizes \(\langle\nabla f(x_k),x-x_k\rangle+\tfrac{1}{2\alpha_k}\lVert x-x_k\rVert_{M_k}^2\) over \(C\). Stop under a prescribed stationarity criterion and return the final feasible iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Take a metric-scaled gradient step and project it onto the feasible set in the same metric; equivalently solve a strongly convex local quadratic model.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable on a neighborhood of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}=P_C^{M_k}(x_k-\alpha_kM_k^{-1}\nabla f(x_k))\in C\).

notation.meaning: projection onto the feasible set in metric M

children.title: Cumulative-Gradient Metrics
children.top_down_role: Scalar, diagonal, and dense metrics built from gradient history.

knowledge_statements.title: Cumulative-Gradient Metrics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar, diagonal, and full-matrix positive metrics accumulated from past gradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For gradients \(g_t\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and regularization \(\delta>0\), cumulative-gradient metrics include the scalar matrix \(H_k^{\mathrm{sc}}=(\delta+\sqrt{\sum_{t=1}^k\lVert g_t\rVert_2^2})I\), the diagonal matrix \(H_k^{\mathrm{diag}}=\operatorname{diag}(\delta+\sqrt{\sum_{t=1}^kg_{t,1}^2},\ldots,\delta+\sqrt{\sum_{t=1}^kg_{t,n}^2})\), and the full matrix \(H_k^{\mathrm{full}}=\delta I+(\sum_{t=1}^kg_tg_t^{\mathsf T})^{1/2}\). Each is positive definite and depends only on gradient history through time \(k\). A metric-scaled step uses \(H_k^{-1}g_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cumulative-gradient scaling uses scalar, coordinatewise, or full-matrix square roots of accumulated gradient energy, regularized to remain invertible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H_k^{\mathrm{sc}}\succ0\), \(H_k^{\mathrm{diag}}\succ0\), and \(H_k^{\mathrm{full}}\succ0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed scalar, diagonal, and full-matrix metrics are plausible AdaGrad conventions, but no source is supplied and conventions differ regarding regularization placement and matrix square roots.

children.title: Adaptive-Regularization Interpretation
children.top_down_role: Cumulative scaling viewed through changing regularization geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive-Regularization Interpretation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric-scaled updates represented as minimizers of changing quadratic regularizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H_k\succ0\), \(g_k=\nabla f(x_k)\), and \(\alpha_k>0\). The update \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_kH_k^{-1}g_k\) is equivalently represented by \[x_{k+1}=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\left\{\langle g_k,x-x_k\rangle+\frac{1}{2\alpha_k}\lVert x-x_k\rVert_{H_k}^2\right\}.\] When \(H_k\) is formed from cumulative gradients, the regularizer changes with the observed gradient geometry: frequently active directions receive larger quadratic penalties and hence smaller subsequent displacement. The equivalence is exact for each fixed positive-definite \(H_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cumulative-metric gradient step exactly minimizes a linearized objective plus a quadratic regularizer whose geometry adapts to past gradients.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_x\{\langle g_k,x-x_k\rangle+(2\alpha_k)^{-1}\lVert x-x_k\rVert_{H_k}^2\}=x_k-\alpha_kH_k^{-1}g_k\).

notation.meaning: norm induced by the adaptive metric

children.title: Online AdaGrad Regret-Theory Boundary
children.top_down_role: Navigation boundary for scalar, coordinatewise, and full-matrix adaptive regret guarantees.

knowledge_statements.title: Online AdaGrad Regret-Theory Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates deterministic smooth descent analysis from adversarial online regret guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For online convex losses \(\ell_t\) on a convex decision set \(C\), regret is \(R_T(u)=\sum_{t=1}^T(\ell_t(x_t)-\ell_t(u))\) for a comparator \(u\in C\). Scalar, diagonal, and full-matrix cumulative-gradient metrics can be analyzed through bounds depending respectively on aggregate, coordinatewise, or directional gradient energy. Such bounds concern a sequence of possibly different losses and comparison with the best fixed decision in hindsight. They do not, without an additional online-to-batch or repeated-objective argument, imply a last-iterate convergence rate for minimizing one smooth deterministic objective. Conversely, deterministic descent estimates do not establish adversarial regret guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: AdaGrad regret bounds address changing online losses and fixed-comparator regret; they do not automatically provide last-iterate rates for one deterministic smooth objective.
assumptions_latex: The algorithm chooses \(x_t\) before observing the current loss or subgradient.
The comparator \(u\) is fixed over the horizon.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{online regret guarantee}\not\Rightarrow\text{deterministic last-iterate convergence rate}\) without an explicit transfer argument.

notation.meaning: regret through horizon T relative to comparator u

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The online-versus-deterministic boundary is well framed and the failure_boundary kind fits, but no authoritative online AdaGrad or online-to-batch source is provided.

children.title: Metric Conditioning Safeguards
children.top_down_role: Controls for singular, ill-conditioned, or excessively anisotropic metrics.

children.title: Metric Regularization
children.top_down_role: Controls that prevent singular or severely ill-conditioned metric choices.

knowledge_statements.title: Metric Regularization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive spectral regularization ensuring invertibility and limiting inverse-step amplification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a symmetric positive-semidefinite raw metric \(G_k\) and parameter \(\delta_k>0\), form \(M_k=G_k+\delta_kI\). Use the regularized direction \(d_k=-M_k^{-1}\nabla f(x_k)\) and update \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kd_k\), subject to the method's stopping rule. Since every eigenvalue is shifted by \(\delta_k\), \(M_k\succeq\delta_kI\) and \(\lVert M_k^{-1}\rVert_2\le1/\delta_k\). Thus the metric is invertible even when \(G_k\) is singular, while large \(\delta_k\) moves the direction toward a uniformly scaled negative gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Add a positive identity multiple to a semidefinite metric, making it invertible and bounding amplification by its inverse.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M_k\succeq\delta_kI\) and \(\lVert M_k^{-1}\rVert_2\le\delta_k^{-1}\).

children.title: Metric Clipping
children.top_down_role: Bounds limiting extreme coordinate scales or spectral values.

knowledge_statements.title: Metric Clipping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spectral projection of a symmetric metric onto prescribed positive-definite bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a symmetric raw metric \(G_k=Q_k\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_{k,1},\ldots,\lambda_{k,n})Q_k^{\mathsf T}\) and constants \(0<\ell\le u<\infty\), define \(\widehat\lambda_{k,i}=\min\{u,\max\{\ell,\lambda_{k,i}\}\}\) and \(M_k=Q_k\operatorname{diag}(\widehat\lambda_{k,1},\ldots,\widehat\lambda_{k,n})Q_k^{\mathsf T}\). Use \(-M_k^{-1}\nabla f(x_k)\) as the scaled direction. Then \(\ell I\preceq M_k\preceq uI\) and \(\kappa_2(M_k)\le u/\ell\). For diagonal metrics, the same operation clips each diagonal entry and requires no eigendecomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Clip every metric eigenvalue to a positive interval, producing a uniformly bounded positive-definite scaling with controlled condition number.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ell I\preceq M_k\preceq uI\) and \(\kappa_2(M_k)\le u/\ell\).

children.title: Metric Safeguard Bias
children.top_down_role: Distortion of curvature adaptation introduced by protective controls.

knowledge_statements.title: Metric Safeguard Bias
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifies how regularization or clipping alters the intended preconditioned direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\succ0\) be a raw metric, let \(M\succ0\) be its safeguarded replacement, and let \(g\in\mathbb{R}^n\). The directional perturbation is \(e=M^{-1}g-G^{-1}g=(M^{-1}-G^{-1})g=M^{-1}(G-M)G^{-1}g\). Consequently, \(\lVert e\rVert_2\le\lVert M^{-1}\rVert_2\lVert M-G\rVert_2\lVert G^{-1}g\rVert_2\). Thus safeguards stabilize inversion but bias the intended scaled direction whenever they modify the metric. If clipping or regularization becomes inactive asymptotically, this perturbation vanishes provided the displayed factors remain controlled; persistent safeguarding can instead produce persistent directional bias.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Safeguards trade stability for distortion: changing the metric changes its inverse-scaled gradient, with an explicit perturbation bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert M^{-1}g-G^{-1}g\rVert_2\le\lVert M^{-1}\rVert_2\lVert M-G\rVert_2\lVert G^{-1}g\rVert_2\).

children.title: Metric Representation Families
children.top_down_role: Scalar, diagonal, structured, low-rank, and dense metric formats.

assumptions_latex: Each represented metric is symmetric positive definite; in the structured low-rank case, \(C_k=C_k^{\mathsf T}\) and \(D_k+U_kC_kU_k^{\mathsf T}\succ0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_k=-M_kg_k\) can be computed from any listed representation without changing the abstract variable-metric iteration.

notation.meaning: positive-definite scaling metric at iteration k

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical finite-dimensional matrix representations used by variable-metric methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical finite-dimensional representations of positive-definite scaling metrics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\ge1\), a symmetric positive-definite metric \(M_k\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^n\) used in the scaled direction \(d_k=-M_kg_k\) may be represented densely by storing its independent entries; diagonally as \(M_k=\operatorname{diag}(m_k)\) with \(m_k\in\mathbb{R}_{++}^n\); scalarly as \(M_k=\gamma_kI\) with \(\gamma_k>0\); in structured low-rank form as \(M_k=D_k+U_kC_kU_k^{\mathsf T}\), where \(D_k\) is positive diagonal, \(U_k\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}\), \(C_k=C_k^{\mathsf T}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times r}\), and the resulting sum is positive definite; or implicitly in limited-memory form, where \(M_kg_k\) is computed from at most \(m\) stored vector pairs without forming \(M_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-definite scaling metric may be represented densely, diagonally, as a scalar identity multiple, by positive-definite structured low-rank data, or implicitly using limited-memory vector pairs.

children.title: Metric Update Costs
children.top_down_role: Computational expense associated with refreshing changing metrics.

knowledge_statements.title: Metric Update Costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arithmetic costs for refreshing common metric representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the unit-cost real-arithmetic model, refreshing every stored parameter of an \(n\)-dimensional metric has cost \(\Theta(n^2)\) for an unstructured dense matrix, \(\Theta(n)\) for a diagonal metric, and \(\Theta(1)\) for a scalar multiple of the identity. Updating an explicitly stored rank-\(r\) factor \(U_k\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}\) costs \(\Theta(nr)\) when all factor entries are refreshed. Appending one curvature pair to a limited-memory representation costs \(\Theta(n)\), excluding gradient evaluation and any separate line search; maintaining at most \(m\) pairs does not alter this per-pair insertion order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dense metrics cost quadratic time to refresh; diagonal and limited-memory pair updates cost linear time; scalar updates cost constant time.
assumptions_latex: Each scalar read, write, and arithmetic operation has unit cost.
A refresh touches every explicitly stored parameter.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The update costs are \(\Theta(n^2)\), \(\Theta(n)\), \(\Theta(1)\), \(\Theta(nr)\), and \(\Theta(n)\) for dense, diagonal, scalar, rank-\(r\), and pair-appending representations, respectively.

notation.meaning: maximum number of stored curvature pairs

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: operation counts follow the number of refreshed representation parameters

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role fits Metric Update Costs and the operation counts are coherent under the stated full-refresh unit-cost model. No inspectable source locator is supplied.

children.title: Metric Storage Costs
children.top_down_role: Memory requirements associated with alternative metric formats.

assumptions_latex: Only representation data are counted; objective data and workspace storage are excluded.
The limited-memory capacity reserves storage for exactly \(m\) vector pairs and at most \(O(m)\) associated scalars.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The storage capacities scale as \(\Theta(n^2)\), \(\Theta(n)\), \(\Theta(1)\), \(\Theta(nr+r^2)\), and \(\Theta(mn)\) for the five respective families.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: storage counts follow directly from explicitly listed scalar parameters
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Storage requirements for common finite-dimensional metric representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Counting real scalars, an unstructured symmetric \(n\times n\) metric requires \(n(n+1)/2=\Theta(n^2)\) storage, a diagonal metric requires \(n=\Theta(n)\), and a scalar metric requires \(1=\Theta(1)\). A representation \(D_k+U_kC_kU_k^{\mathsf T}\), with diagonal \(D_k\), \(U_k\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}\), and dense symmetric \(C_k\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times r}\), requires \(n+nr+r(r+1)/2=\Theta(nr+r^2)\) scalars. Capacity for exactly \(m\) curvature pairs in \(\mathbb{R}^n\), together with at most \(O(m)\) associated scalars, requires \(2mn+O(m)=\Theta(mn)\) scalars.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dense storage is quadratic, diagonal storage linear, scalar storage constant, low-rank storage depends on dimension and rank, and capacity for a fixed number of limited-memory pairs is proportional to memory depth times dimension.
knowledge_statements.title: Metric Storage Costs

children.title: Structure–Cost Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Balance between curvature expressiveness and implementation expense.

assumptions_latex: The same target pair \((H,g)\) is used for both families.
Storage and arithmetic are compared using the explicit representation and unit-cost models stated in the prerequisite cost records.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e(\mathcal{M}_2;H,g)\le e(\mathcal{M}_1;H,g)\); any accompanying increase in computational cost must be assessed from the representations used for the two families.

notation.meaning: best directional approximation error over a metric family

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: approximation monotonicity follows from minimization over nested sets; representation costs require an explicit cost model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximation and computational tradeoffs induced by restricting the metric representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal{M}_1\subseteq\mathcal{M}_2\subseteq\mathbb{S}_{++}^n\), and for \(H\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^n\) and \(g\in\mathbb{R}^n\) define \(e(\mathcal{M};H,g)=\inf_{M\in\mathcal{M}}\lVert(M-H)g\rVert_2\). Then \(e(\mathcal{M}_2;H,g)\le e(\mathcal{M}_1;H,g)\). Thus enlarging the admissible family cannot worsen the best attainable scaled-direction fit. When the larger family is implemented with additional dense entries, factor columns, or stored vector pairs, its storage and arithmetic costs are those of that richer representation and may exceed the costs of a scalar, diagonal, lower-rank, or shorter-memory implementation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A larger admissible metric family cannot have worse best directional approximation error. Its computational cost may be higher when its implementation stores or updates more representation data.

children.title: Nonlinear Conjugate-Gradient Foundations
children.top_down_role: The transition from quadratic conjugacy to nonlinear direction recurrences.

children.title: Quadratic Conjugate-Direction Model
children.top_down_role: The linear-quadratic template motivating nonlinear extensions.

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Conjugate-Direction Model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear conjugate-gradient template for a strictly convex quadratic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(A=A^{\mathsf T}\succ0\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}^n\), minimize \(q(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Ax-b^{\mathsf T}x\). Set \(g_0=Ax_0-b\) and \(d_0=-g_0\). While \(g_k\ne0\), compute \(\alpha_k=-g_k^{\mathsf T}d_k/(d_k^{\mathsf T}Ad_k)\), \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kd_k\), \(g_{k+1}=Ax_{k+1}-b\), \(\beta_{k+1}=\|g_{k+1}\|_2^2/\|g_k\|_2^2\), and \(d_{k+1}=-g_{k+1}+\beta_{k+1}d_k\). Stop when \(g_k=0\) and output \(x_k\); in exact arithmetic this occurs within at most \(n\) iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear conjugate gradient minimizes a positive-definite quadratic using exact line searches and mutually conjugate directions, terminating within the dimension in exact arithmetic.
assumptions_latex: Arithmetic and matrix-vector products are exact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output equals \(x_\star=A^{-1}b\), and nonzero generated directions satisfy \(d_i^{\mathsf T}Ad_j=0\) for \(i\ne j\).

notation.meaning: quadratic gradient at the kth iterate

children.title: Nonlinear Direction-Recurrence Framework
children.top_down_role: The common structural organizer for nonlinear conjugate-gradient updates.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonlinear Direction-Recurrence Framework
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shared recurrence underlying standard nonlinear conjugate-gradient methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For continuously differentiable \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), choose \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}^n\), set \(g_0=\nabla f(x_0)\), and set \(d_0=-g_0\). At iteration \(k\), choose a positive line-search step \(\alpha_k\), update \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kd_k\), evaluate \(g_{k+1}=\nabla f(x_{k+1})\), select a method-specific coefficient \(\beta_{k+1}\), and set \(d_{k+1}=-g_{k+1}+\beta_{k+1}d_k\). Stop when a prescribed condition such as \(\|g_k\|_2\le\varepsilon\) holds; otherwise output the final iterate after the allowed iteration budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonlinear conjugate-gradient methods share a gradient-plus-previous-direction recurrence and differ mainly in their coefficient and line-search safeguards.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every standard nonlinear conjugate-gradient variant is obtained by specifying \(\beta_{k+1}\), the line search, and any restart or truncation rule in this recurrence.

children.title: Exact-Search Quadratic Equivalences
children.top_down_role: Coincidences among update families in the ideal quadratic regime.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact-Search Quadratic Equivalences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coefficient coincidences for exact line search on a positive-definite quadratic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Ax-b^{\mathsf T}x\) with \(A=A^{\mathsf T}\succ0\), and generate \(d_{k+1}=-g_{k+1}+\beta_{k+1}d_k\) using exact minimization of \(f(x_k+\alpha d_k)\). Before termination, the gradients are mutually orthogonal and successive directions are \(A\)-conjugate. Consequently, whenever their denominators are nonzero, the Fletcher–Reeves, Polak–Ribiere–Polyak, Hestenes–Stiefel, Dai–Yuan, and Hager–Zhang formulas produce the same \(\beta_{k+1}\) as linear conjugate gradient. Hence all five recurrences generate identical iterates and directions in exact arithmetic from the same \(x_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a positive-definite quadratic with exact line searches, the principal nonlinear conjugate-gradient coefficients coincide with linear conjugate gradient.
assumptions_latex: Every line search is exact and arithmetic is exact.
All displayed coefficient denominators are nonzero before termination.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\beta_{k+1}^{\mathrm{FR}}=\beta_{k+1}^{\mathrm{PRP}}=\beta_{k+1}^{\mathrm{HS}}=\beta_{k+1}^{\mathrm{DY}}=\beta_{k+1}^{\mathrm{HZ}}\), and the corresponding iterates coincide.

children.title: Fletcher-Reeves Family
children.top_down_role: Norm-ratio nonlinear conjugate-gradient variants.

knowledge_statements.title: Fletcher-Reeves Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Norm-ratio nonlinear conjugate-gradient update.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Within the nonlinear recurrence, define \(g_k=\nabla f(x_k)\), choose \(d_0=-g_0\), and after obtaining \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kd_k\), set \(\beta_{k+1}^{\mathrm{FR}}=\|g_{k+1}\|_2^2/\|g_k\|_2^2\) whenever \(g_k\ne0\). Then set \(d_{k+1}=-g_{k+1}+\beta_{k+1}^{\mathrm{FR}}d_k\). A restarted Fletcher–Reeves member replaces this coefficient by zero when its prescribed restart test fires. Stop and output \(x_k\) when \(\|g_k\|_2\le\varepsilon\), or after the iteration budget is exhausted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fletcher–Reeves scales the previous direction by the ratio of successive squared gradient norms, optionally resetting that coefficient at restarts.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The next direction is \(d_{k+1}=-g_{k+1}+(\|g_{k+1}\|_2^2/\|g_k\|_2^2)d_k\), unless a restart sets the coefficient to zero.

knowledge_statements.title: Polak-Ribiere-Polyak Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gradient-difference update and its nonnegative truncation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g_k=\nabla f(x_k)\), \(y_k=g_{k+1}-g_k\), and \(d_0=-g_0\). After a positive line-search step, define \(\beta_{k+1}^{\mathrm{PRP}}=g_{k+1}^{\mathsf T}y_k/\|g_k\|_2^2\) when \(g_k\ne0\), and set \(d_{k+1}=-g_{k+1}+\beta_{k+1}^{\mathrm{PRP}}d_k\). The PRP-plus modification uses \(\beta_{k+1}^{\mathrm{PRP+}}=\max\{0,\beta_{k+1}^{\mathrm{PRP}}\}\), thereby restarting to steepest descent whenever the untruncated coefficient is negative. Stop at \(\|g_k\|_2\le\varepsilon\) or the iteration limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: PRP uses the new gradient paired with the gradient difference; PRP-plus truncates negative coefficients to trigger a steepest-descent restart.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: PRP and PRP-plus use the same recurrence, with coefficients \(g_{k+1}^{\mathsf T}y_k/\|g_k\|_2^2\) and \(\max\{0,g_{k+1}^{\mathsf T}y_k/\|g_k\|_2^2\}\), respectively.

knowledge_statements.title: Hestenes-Stiefel Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direction-curvature-scaled nonlinear conjugate-gradient update.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g_k=\nabla f(x_k)\), \(y_k=g_{k+1}-g_k\), and \(d_0=-g_0\). After obtaining \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kd_k\), define \(\beta_{k+1}^{\mathrm{HS}}=g_{k+1}^{\mathsf T}y_k/(d_k^{\mathsf T}y_k)\) whenever \(d_k^{\mathsf T}y_k\ne0\), and set \(d_{k+1}=-g_{k+1}+\beta_{k+1}^{\mathrm{HS}}d_k\). Safeguarded members may truncate or restart this coefficient when the denominator is too small or the resulting direction fails a prescribed descent test. Stop at the gradient tolerance or iteration limit.

knowledge_statements.title: Hager-Zhang Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hager–Zhang update with a sufficient-descent safeguard.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g_k=\nabla f(x_k)\), \(y_k=g_{k+1}-g_k\), and suppose \(d_k^{\mathsf T}y_k\ne0\). Define \(\beta_{k+1}^{\mathrm{HZ}}=((y_k-2d_k\|y_k\|_2^2/(d_k^{\mathsf T}y_k))^{\mathsf T}g_{k+1})/(d_k^{\mathsf T}y_k)\). A safeguarded Hager–Zhang update sets \(\beta_{k+1}=\max\{\beta_{k+1}^{\mathrm{HZ}},\eta_k\}\), where \(\eta_k=-1/(\|d_k\|_2\min\{\eta,\|g_k\|_2\})\) for fixed \(\eta>0\), and then uses \(d_{k+1}=-g_{k+1}+\beta_{k+1}d_k\). The line search and safeguard are chosen to maintain sufficient descent; stop at the gradient tolerance or iteration limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hager–Zhang combines a gradient-difference coefficient with a lower safeguard designed to preserve sufficiently descending directions under compatible line searches.
